subtopic: ALLEGED APPOINTMENT TO COMMISSION WITHOUT CONSULTATION WITH ORGANIZED LABOUR
speechtext:
Last Friday I announced the appointment of Alastair F. MacArthur, former president of the Ontario federation of labour, as labour representative on the unemployment insurance commission. This appointment has since been described by Mr. Claude Jodoin, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, as "political patronage" and a violation of the consultative clause in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I deny both these charges, Mr. Speaker. First, on the principle of consultation, I may say I discussed the whole matter with Mr. Jodoin on January 30. Again, I may say there was considerable correspondence on the matter in which I asked Mr. Jodoin for nominations and in which he submitted three names. The names submitted by Mr. Jodoin were presented to cabinet and were given the fullest consideration. In addition the name of Mr. MacArthur was submitted, as I had told Mr. Jodoin it would be. Thus, Mr. Speaker, there was full consultation with Mr. Jodoin all along the line. The principle of consultation was carried out and will continue to be carried out. However, it must

be made clear that no single group will have an exclusive power of veto over cabinet appointments.
As to Mr. MacArthur's political affiliation, Mr. Speaker, I believe he has already made a statement attesting that he has not been a member of any political party. This should be sufficient. I may say that the question of political affiliation was first brought forward not by myself but by Mr. Jodoin. I may say also that I never questioned the political affiliations of his nominees.
I maintain that Mr. MacArthur's record in the labour movement is the best answer to the charge. As president of the Ontario federation of labour from 1946 to 1956 Mr. MacArthur achieved distinguished eminence in the ranks of labour, and in 1954 was one of three candidates for leadership of the Trades and Labour Congress. He was defeated by Mr. Jodoin. As international representative of the office employees he is familiar with the opinions of labour and the needs of labour. I am sure he will serve with distinction on the unemployment insurance commission. Mr. MacArthur's appointment compares favourably with this government's appointment of Mr. Cleve Kidd to the royal commission on price spreads and the appointment of Mr. Eugene Forsey to the board of broadcast governors. Neither of these men could be described as supporters of the Conservative party.
Over the week end I received and accepted, as a consequence of this appointment, the resignations of Mr. George Burt, Mr. A. An-dras and Mr. Jean Marchand from the unemployment insurance advisory committee. Mr. Burt is head of the united automobile workers; Mr. Andras is chief of the legislation department of the congress; and Mr. Marchand is secretary general of the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour. Like Mr. Jodoin's three nominees for this appointment, all have a record of close affiliation with a political group-not the Progressive Conservative party. I say that political considerations were not absent in these resignations.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that Mr. MacArthur was appointed in the sincere conviction that, having in mind the suitability of all the names put forward-and there were five in all-he would do the best possible job in the interests of organized labour. No other consideration was involved. Already I am pleased to say that I have had ample evidence that it is in this light that this appointment is being viewed by representative labour groups in this country.

subsubtopic: U.S. INTERFERENCE WITH CANADIAN TRUCKS IN TRANSIT
speechtext: May I direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the Canadian government protested to the United States government about the interference by United States authorities with Canadian trucks in transit from British Columbia to other parts of Canada via the state of Washington? If so, what was the nature and result of such protests?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: U.S. INTERFERENCE WITH CANADIAN TRUCKS IN TRANSIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. gentleman for giving notice of this question. I think possibly in order that the record may be clear I might be permitted to refer in general to what actually took place, and also to the representation to the United States which was made by the government.
On February 19, Gill-Pix Express Lines were stopped by United States customs from passing their trucks in bond through the United States because they were suspected of

transporting goods being imported from mainland China. The company made representations to the United States authorities, and at a later date the problem was drawn to the attention of the Department of External Affairs by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway.
A letter was sent from the department to the United States embassy pointing out that the trade agreement between Canada and the United States, that is the general agreement on tariffs and trade, provided that there should be freedom of transit through the territory of each contracting party regardless of the place of origin of the goods being transported. The United States embassy was asked why this provision did not ensure the right of Canadian trucking firms to pass their trucks through the United States in bond regardless of the origin of the goods being shipped.
The United States embassy has since replied to the letter from the department and indicated that since the beginning of the Korean hostilities there had been an embargo by the United States authorities on all commercial relations between the United States and mainland China, including the use of transit facilities for goods from mainland China. It is, I understand, the view of the United States authorities that the action they have been taken is in accordance with the general agreement on tariffs and trade, article XXI, which reads in part:
Nothing in the agreement shall be construed . . . to prevent any contracting party from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests . . . taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations-
That is the end of the quotation, in part, from the general agreement. The emergency which is deemed by the United States to be in existence is the emergency which originated with the Korean war. The wording of this provision of GATT seems to make it clear that each contracting party is the sole judge of what is to be regarded as the protection of its own security interests within its own country.
However, full consideration is being given as to what action can be appropriately taken by the Canadian authorities in the circumstances. The matter has been brought to the attention of the United States authorities and Canada's viewpoint has been expressed. That viewpoint is that while there is in fact the section of GATT on which reliance is placed, it is the opinion of the Canadian government that the action taken does not fall within the ambit of the section in question.

subsubtopic: U.S. INTERFERENCE WITH CANADIAN TRUCKS IN TRANSIT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could I ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question. In view of what he has just said in reference to United States security, I think it would be of interest to all of us if the Prime Minister would And out how United States security is involved in transporting in bond from one Canadian port to another soya sauce and shrimps.

Mr. Chairman in listening to the comments the minister made specifically in reply to questions raised regarding income tax deductions for transportation costs and

Income Tax Act
for board and lodging where a person has to work and maintain two homes, and for protective work clothing, I came to the conclusion that the Liberal government was the most inept one we have had for many years. The more I listened to my friend the hon. member for Essex East the more I became convinced that the Tory government is just about as bad, because over the years with respect to these very valid submissions regarding deductions for working people they have replied that the matter was under study, that briefs had already been presented, that they were fully aware of the situation, and remarks of that nature.
The minister made a most astounding comment about this the other day, when he said in effect that as far as deductible transportation costs are concerned the time is not now ripe to do this; that we cannot do it in view of the increase in the deficit, the extended borrowings of the government, the increased taxation it has been necessary to impose, and so on. Because of the inability of the minister and his government to cope with these problems he now says that the working man will have to suffer a little longer because the government cannot do these things now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.

No, the minister would not commit himself in such direct words, but that is in effect what the minister said and that is the interpretation many working people will place upon his remarks. Certainly he made reference to the increase in debt that has taken place under his administration. He made reference to the increased taxation, and that is certainly the responsibility of the minister and his colleagues. He also made reference to the declining economy and the other difficulties experienced since he became minister and his colleagues formed the government. There is no question at all but that the working man will have to suffer a little longer under onerous taxation and will not be able to get these justifiable deductions.
The minister made much use of the word "discrimination" and explained how he and his government were concerned with the elimination of discriminatory taxation measures. The minister was not so careful about the question of discrimination in the session preceding the 1958 election, because at that time under his guidance changes were made in the Income Tax Act which cannot be described as other than discriminatory. The amendments made at that time applied to one group of workers only and not to others. I refer to the changes made with

respect to construction employees. What could be more discriminatory and inequitable than that?
I should like to relate the manner in which these amendments were applied. They relate to construction employees, and this situation could arise and probably has arisen. I refer again to logging camps. An employee driving a cat, a bulldozer, working on construction in a logging camp, could fall within the provisions of the act relating to deductions, exemptions, and so on. Another employee working for the same company, driving exactly the same type of bulldozer, exactly the same size, horsepower and everything else, skidding logs out of the bush, would not be allowed such deductions. What could be more discriminatory than that? Certainly if the minister had been more careful in what he was doing prior to the 1958 election, and had not been concerned so much with gathering votes for the Conservatives, we would not have had this kind of inequality that exists today.
What we are asking him to do is to extend the same principle that he endorsed and adopted just a little over a year ago. We are asking him to extend that self-same principle to other groups of workmen in this country. The answer is that the time is not now ripe. When we take this answer with his answers to other proposals we are not too clear on just what is meant, but it is just not acceptable. Certainly it is not acceptable to the working people involved.
If the minister would consult one of his own supporters-I am not sure whether he is in the committee at the moment-if the minister would consult the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who also knows the logging industry very well, having worked in that industry for a number of years, he would get a clear definition and a clear explanation of the effect of the taxation provisions that he says he cannot change. He would get a clear explanation of the effects on the loggers. He does not have to take my word for the tremendously high expenses of the loggers. I am referring to them at the moment because of my familiarity with the high transportation costs of loggers. The minister could get from one of his colleagues in his own party a clear explanation of the extra expenses that workingmen have to bear because provision is not made in the logging industry, in the construction and other camps for families. There are members of the minister's own party who will explain to him in a clear and lucid way the necessity of making these particular deductions that I have been advocating.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on the budget resolutions I want to say first that I think the increased taxes are very high. It we commit excesses in life, whether physical or financial, there comes a day of reckoning, and the day of reckoning for this government has come. This is the second evidence we have of the day of reckoning. The first evidence we had was the increase in the interest rates, and that increase is still going on. Today the minister is handing the Canadian people part of the bill. He is handing them a little less than half the bill, because there is still some $400 million left to pay at some later date.
The minister has said that the tax increases are moderate. They may seem moderate because he has been dealing with billions, but they are very sizable indeed, and they are taking the corporations for a ride. The tax is equal to the highest income tax they have paid at any recent time in peacetime. After all, the extra bill of $352 million is very large indeed. It is equal to about 75 per cent of the total budget in 1939, and over and above that he has $400 million left for which he has given an I.O.U. which exceeds three-quarters of the total budget for 1939.
It is hard to conceive that this government will ever pay any part of that $400 million, because the sum total of the surpluses or savings of the Conservative party since confederation is less than the interest on that $400 million for only one year. In other words, the interest on that $400 million for a year will be $16 million at 4 per cent and their total surpluses since confederation have amounted to only $15 million. The Conservatives have always been the party of debts and deficits, but the old line Tory was a piker when you consider him in relation to the present Diefenbaker Tories, if the present Minister of Finance is to be taken as a criterion. But even he has slowed up lately, and I think he has slowed up because the people have refused to give him money as rapidly as he requires it.
The increase in personal and corporation income tax amounts to $60 million this year, and this is just enough to pay off that part of the conversion loan that did not need to be converted but was converted. Next year the added revenue from the corporation tax and the personal income tax will amount to $110 million. This year it takes $106 million extra to service our debt, and next year nobody knows how much it will amount to. It certainly will be away up. Hon. members can see that the increase in the corporation tax and the personal income tax will not at any time quite measure up to the amount
Income Tax Act
required to service the increase in the public debt. As hon. members know, that has been made up of our deficits and by the minister fooling around with bonds and converting them before they needed to be converted.
We hear all kinds of stories about the minister leaving the portfolio of finance. If he does he will leave this financial mess on the lap of the Prime Minister, and Fleming's folly will become Diefenbaker's debt.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must remind the hon. member that we are not talking about taxation in general. At the present time, we are talking about the Income Tax Act. It would be appreciated by the Chair if the hon. member would limit his remarks to the resolution under discussion at the present time and not extend them into something else.

Mr. Chairman, I accept your ruling except that the other night the Minister of Finance, in speaking on this very same resolution, referred to the clearing of brush from land. He referred to housing; he referred to the dark days of the last administration, and he also referred to the high intelligence of the hon. member for Essex East. Certainly the other speakers in the debate were allowed to go on and traverse more than you are allowing me to discuss at the present time. If you say I cannot touch on interest rates I will forgo that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, so the point may be clearly understood and for the benefit of other hon. members who may choose to speak on this resolution, I think while there was a good deal of latitude taken by hon. members who spoke on this resolution on Thursday evening, the hon. member is now going into a field which is quite beyond what would be in order on this resolution, because he is now trespassing on a field on which the house has already spoken at the present session.
You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that a week ago today we had a supply motion and an amendment was introduced, to be found at page 3073 of Hansard, which included among other things the conversion loan, the bank rate, expansion of the money supply, the national debt and public debt charges, and in a vote on April 28 the house dealt with that amendment and defeated it. So it seems to me that for that reason debate on this question is precluded. It is not a question of latitude in debate last Thursday evening. It is a question of this subject, on which the hon. member is now proposing to speak, having been decided by the house six days ago.

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind hon. members that sins of omission committed at a previous sitting of the house would not justify the Chair in allowing debate on the question under discussion at present to become irrelevant. We cannot debate all over again what has already been debated at length in the house. If only for the sake of preventing constant repetition it is quite important that we adhere to the rule of relevancy as much as possible. It is appreciated by the Chair that it is quite easy in a debate such as the present one, involving the discussion of resolutions which offer a great deal of scope and cover all kinds of matters, to wander afield to some extent, but it would be appreciated by the Chair if hon. members would try as best they can to limit their remarks to the resolution under discussion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want to dispute the ruling you have made. I agree with your ruling in essence and I do not think the house will want to see a debate on this resolution such as was had on the budget or again on the motion to go into supply. Surely it is not our intention to do that. But may I point out with respect to Your Honour that what the hon. member for Welland was doing was to discuss interest so far as the tax yield is concerned, and if he limits himself to that aspect of the matter I submit that he is perfectly in order.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to go back to the resolution itself, but I just wanted to say that the increases in the income and corporation taxes were almost exactly enough to take care of the increased charges on our national debt. The Minister of Finance has given us three reasons for the rise in interest rates and, in so far as that affects the money that we should raise, I think he should tell us which one is right. In other words, the other night he spent an hour or so telling us that the government had nothing to do with the rise in interest rates. In the budget speech he said that too many bonds on the market created an upward pressure on interest rates. Again, last November he came into the house and said that the government had achieved a decrease in interest rates. He has given us these three explanations. He should get up and tell us which one is right. They cannot all be right.
In my opinion he has lost the art of achievement, and having lost that art I can well realize why the Prime Minister would think he would be a good secretary of state for external affairs. It is unfortunate that the minister has to raise taxes at this time, particularly when the government promised that taxes would be reduced. They went all over the country, certainly all over Ontario, and said they were going to increase social

benefits and reduce taxes. Any time I heard them on the radio that was what they were saying. They said that when the Liberals were in power they were collecting too much in taxes, but now they are collecting more themselves.
The corporation income tax is increased. That was referred to the other night, and if I can close my remarks by dealing with corporation income tax I will not speak on paragraph No. 2 of the resolution unless I am restricted now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order, may I suggest to the hon. member that it might be more convenient to discuss the corporation tax on the next item. At the outset it was agreed by the committee, I believe, that it would make for an orderly discussion if the paragraphs of the resolution were called one at a time, and that matter obviously touches on the second paragraph.
I agree.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we proceed to paragraph 2?

No, I do not think that is fair. I think the Minister of Finance will agree that on Thursday night I was as fair as anybody could possibly be when I suggested that in past sessions on such resolutions it had been indicated by the Chair that in committee we must consider with the strictest of relevancy the individual items as worded in the resolution. In my own remarks I confined myself to items that were enumerated in the resolution. The committee was allowed to wander. I suggested that we do as has been done in past years and that at a certain stage we confine our attention to subsidiary paragraphs in the resolution.
That was not done. Mr. Chairman, you are not the chairman who was here on Thursday night, but because of what went on the year before I did have some words with him after the event which I am sure he will not mind me speaking about. The hon. member for Welland is discussing the proposal that we increases taxes on personal and corporation income, and in subsequent paragraphs there are other forms of taxation all involving a considerable amount of money.
The hon. member for Welland was asserting that had certain improvident actions not been taken these new imposts might not have been necessary, and I say this is a very relevant matter for the committee to discuss because personal income taxes are to be raised by $54 million and corporation taxes by $56 million under these two paragraphs of the general resolution.
I only ask for consistency. If the committee as a whole is prepared to direct its

attention solely to paragraph 1 of the resolution I think that is satisfactory, but the hon. member for Welland has said very properly that one of the reasons for imposing additional taxation is the improvident and unnecessary spending such as occurred with respect to the conversion loan and under other headings.

Mr. Chairman, when the resolution came up the other night the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River did stick to paragraph No. 1, but no other member who spoke did so. That is why I wanted to get a ruling from the Chair as to whether I can go on and speak about corporation taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I draw attention to what was said at the outset of the discussion on the evening of April 30, at page 3209 of Hansard. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River opened the discussion by asking me if I had any comment to make beyond the budget address. In reply I said:
Mr. Chairman, I think there is nothing new to be mentioned in connection with this opening paragraph. When we come down to paragraph 9, Mr. Chairman, I will have an amendment to propose to it. If I may make a suggestion in the interest of orderly procedure, while there is just one resolution to amend the Income Tax Act it might contribute to orderly discussion in the committee if you were to call the paragraphs seriatim.
Then the deputy chairman said:
Is the committee agreeable that the paragraphs be discussed seriatim?
I understood, Mr. Chairman, that was the basis upon which we proceeded. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River then spoke, and on page 3212 of Hansard for that date you will see that the chairman asked:
Is there any further discussion on paragraph 1?
My understanding was that the suggestion of following the paragraphs one by one in the order in which they are printed commended itself to the committee as one that would make for orderly procedure. The first paragraph, of course, relates to the proposed increase in personal income tax, the second paragraph to the proposed increase in the corporation tax. If it is, as indicated, the intention of the hon. member for Welland to discuss the corporation tax, I would think it would contribute to orderly discussion if we could take one paragraph at a time and make sure that before we launched into a discussion of the proposed changes in the corporation tax we had cleared up the proposed changes in the personal income tax. Otherwise, if we are going to scatter our observations widely over the various matters covered by these nine paragraphs I do not think we are going to have an orderly and
Income Tax Act
consecutive discussion. This is not a suggestion that will curtail debate.

May I add that it was the understanding of this group that the paragraphs were going to be taken seriatim, and if any change were made in that understanding then certainly we would like to know about it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is the understanding of the Chair that each paragraph is to be discussed separately. Actually the Chair does not wish to be too severe on anyone during this debate, but for the sake of orderly discussion each matter should be discussed in separate form.
In answer to the request of the hon. member for Welland I can only say that we should try to discuss each item as it is listed here. In other words, if he would discuss the personal income tax before the corporation tax, then we would have an orderly discussion. Whether or not the Chair rules that what the hon. member is saying is out of order depends entirely upon what the hon. member may say. However, for the sake of orderly procedure we should cover each item thoroughly, and it would be appreciated if hon. members adhered to this ruling.
I shall be glad to delay my remarks, Mr. Chairman; however, I would say that if I had been allowed to go on for two minutes we would have saved time.

There is one question I should like to address to the minister, if I may, before we proceed. It concerns item 1 and is related to the question I discussed the other evening, that is the exemptions or deductions for certain classes of workers. I find in volume 2 of Hansard for 1957-58, starting right at the bottom of page 2004 and extending on to page 2005, there are some remarks by the minister regarding one of the proposed changes in the Income Tax Act as it related to construction employees. I would preface my question by reading the remarks of the minister in explanation of this change. He said:
Briefly it will provide that if the construction site is so distant that the worker cannot reasonably be expected to return daily to his normal place of residence where he maintains a home in which he lives with his wife or some dependent person, then the construction employee will not be required to include in his income for tax purposes the value of the free board and lodging or reasonable allowances paid to him to cover expenses of meals and lodging, or the value of travelling expenses paid by the employer in transporting him to the site and back home again.
I wonder what the present view of the minister would be. In commenting on these proposals the other day he said that the suggestion as to what was required was not

Income Tax Act
too clear. Would the minister comment on the difficulties if the provision which already exists in the act with regard to construction employees were to be extended to include other employees who are in precisely the same position?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. member will read the whole of the debate during the fall session of 1957 he will find that there was quite an extensive discussion preceding the amendment that is now to be found as section 5, subsection 2 of the Income Tax Act. It was quite clear at that time that in the face of the strong representations that had been made and in the light of the history of the way in which the claims of construction workers in respect of travelling expenses had been handled by my predecessors, there was a case for introducing this particular amendment giving the right to construction workers to claim exemptions. The hon. member will see there a reference to the fact that this exemption had been accorded to construction workers until the previous year. We were, in effect, dealing with a situation where a practice which had been in existence for a long time was in the course of being reversed under a decision that had been made before we came into office, and having regard to that long history and the strong representations that had been made, not only by the construction industry but by unions of workers in that industry, we asked parliament to enact a provision which would have the effect of maintaining a practice that had obtained until 1957.
Parliament gave effect to that proposal. The case of the logging workers was raised at that time. I tried to make it very clear that there would be difficulty in applying this new legislation, and that there would be borderline cases which would make it almost of necessity a provision difficult of application and that we would be guided by experience. It was made clear that the position of the logging worker and our experience in the application of section 5, subsection 2 of the act would be studied to see if this matter could be worked out in the end in a way that would avoid any possibility of discrimination.
Now, I might say that in general the view that was expressed at that time has been largely borne out in practice. The section has been widely resorted to by numbers of persons who are construction workers. There have been borderline cases and there have been some difficulties. The Department of National Revenue has proceeded to give a reasonable interpretation to the provisions enacted when this matter was last under discussion.

I must say, Mr. Chairman, that our experience has not yet reached the point where we could undertake to ask that even comparable provisions, let alone similar provisions, could be entertained in favour of certain other groups of workers. The legislation to which I referred does not permit a worker to deduct his own expenses. The legislation rather provides that he is not obliged to bring into his income payments that are provided by his employer for transportation, meals and lodging.

If I may say so, Mr. Chairman, I do not think I was confused over the application of the legislation. That is the way I understood it applied, as just indicated by the minister. But if this provision had been in effect, as the minister said, for a number of years and then was altered in 1957, I take it, and then revised again or revived-probably that is the right word- by the amendment to the Income Tax Act in the 1957-58 session, surely after it had been in effect for that period of time the department should have had sufficient experience to allow them to extend the selfsame principle to other types of employees. I cannot see too much difficulty about it.
I will relate again the instance in a logging camp. Under the application of the section-and I am talking about the west coast of British Columbia again because of my familiarity with the situation there-if a person goes out to work as a bulldozer operator on the construction phase of a logging camp's operation, he then comes within the provision just related by the minister. But if that same person happens to go out to work and drives the same type of bulldozer, exactly the same operation, but performs some other duties such as dragging logs out of the bush, he does not come under it. What could be more discriminatory than that situation?
What would be the difficulty in applying the self-same provision which applies to construction employees to, say, cook and bunk-house workers or cooks, bakers and so on in logging camp cook houses who receive, with respect to free board and lodging, exactly the same consideration as do construction employees, yet have to pay tax on it? What is the difficulty in extending it to a person in a mining camp where there are bunkhouses and so on? I do not refer to some of the more settled camps where large numbers of families live and which in effect are settled cities or towns. I refer to those out in the hills far from community life, transportation and so on where they have bunkhouses, where exactly the same type of situation exists, where a person can be a construction employee and

receive the benefits just outlined by the minister. He may get transferred to another job and be in precisely the same position with respect to board and lodging and transportation, yet not receive the benefits under that provision.
After the many years of experience which the department has had in administering, as the minister said, the application of this arrangement to construction employees, surely they have been derelict in their duty if they have not been able to find out how to apply it to other types of employees. I would appreciate a fuller explanation by the minister as to what difficulties he is talking about which stand in the way of extending this provision to other types of employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
From the hon.
member's own remarks it is quite evident that he is aware that if it were extended to loggers as a group we could not stop there, but would be obliged to extend it to other groups and it would just go on and on. Where the line would ever be drawn I do not for the life of me know. I referred to a particular situation which gave rise to the amendment that was introduced in late 1957 because of the history that preceded it. Here was a situation in which in the past the act had been administered in such a way that construction workers had not been required to bring into their income payments received by them from their employers by way of transportation, meals and lodging. That was a particular situation. The representations which we had received and which commended themselves to parliament a year and a half ago were put on that basis, namely the construction worker. At that time we had representations made by some hon. members who said, "Why do you not apply this provision to the logging worker?" We went into this matter at some length. The discussion was extended at that time. I would invite my hon. friend to refer to that discussion, where these matters were discussed from both sides of the house.
The fact is that the situation is not any easier from the point of view of enforcement than we contemplated it might be. The immediate context, I would remind the hon. member, was a history under which construction workers had not been required to include in their income transportation, board and lodging. Again that was a situation that had an immediate context as well, because this matter was brought to a head in relation to construction workers employed on one of the defence lines; I think it was the mid-Canada line at that time.
Income Tax Act
We had representations after that. Some organizations came to us and said, "If this provision is not capable of general application, then you ought to take it away from the construction workers". We had representations to that effect from some labour organizations. We felt that, parliament having enacted this particular provision, under the circumstances the matter should be given an opportunity for a fair test, and that is the situation that exists now.

If I may, I should like to make one other comment on that matter. The other evening, when the broader application of the suggestions I had to make was being discussed -notably transportation, clothing, maintenance of two homes and so on-for deduction purposes, the minister then said it was impossible to legislate for a select group of workers. He did not want to have any part of that suggestion because that was discrimination. He now turns around and says, "We believe in discrimination; we believe in legislating for a select group of workers as opposed to other workers".
That is precisely what he is saying. He has set up a preferred group of workers in so far as income tax provisions are concerned, notably construction employees. I am not decrying the fact that that should happen. I am merely saying that it does not seem sensible, especially after this provision has been in effect for so many years and especially after the minister said that he does not believe in discrimination and could not possibly make any provision in respect to loggers, miners and all these other types of employees who find that these excessive costs must be met. When he said he could not legislate discriminatorily in that way it does not seem sensible for him to turn around and justify the maintenance of something which has been in effect for so many years and which is in effect discriminatory against all other types of employee.
It is just silly. Surely the minister can apply himself or the officials of his department can apply themselves more directly to this problem in the hope of finding a solution to it. It does not seem impossible. If the minister would sit down and concern himself more with the application of this provision than he does with these other questions, or would get some of the officials in his department to apply themselves to the problem, it is not insurmountable. If that had been done at the time of the reinstatement of the provision for construction employees; if a start had been made on it then, I am sure that at this stage we could have had an acceptably workable statutory provision which would put working class people on a fairly equitable basis, instead

Income Tax Act
of setting up a preferred group and discriminating against the rest. The minister speaks out of both sides of his mouth. He says he does not believe in discrimination and cannot legislate for a select group of employees, and then turns around and says that in this case he should do so.

May I add a word or two. I believe the Minister of Finance is a family man. No doubt he likes to be with his family once in a while, and he realizes the cost of being separated for a long time. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I think this is perhaps what the hon. member for Port Arthur had in mind the other day when he spoke about salaries for members of parliament, but we are not discussing that matter at the moment.
We are now discussing a situation where, particularly on the west coast of this country, because of our economy workers are separated from their families when engaged in industry and construction, in our fisheries, in logging and in mining. When one is separated from one's family there is a big cost in transportation involved, and one is actually placed in the position of maintaining two homes at one time. He has to maintain the home where his family is and the place where he works and pays board.
That is why I started out by saying that I understood the Minister of Finance was a family man and would like to see his wife and kiddies once in a while. Then as his kiddies grow up and become men and women, he would like to see his grandchildren. Is it not therefore understandable that the people in a province which contributes a good deal in monetary value to the treasury of this country, because they are engaged in logging, mining and construction, also do not like maintaining two family homes and like to be able to get home once in a while? Surely the Minister of Finance will agree that having worked out certain rights for employees in the construction industry two years ago, he should now apply the same general principle to those engaged in the logging and mining industries of British Columbia.
I was going to ask the Minister of Finance if he would just get that red blood flowing a little faster through his veins and see if he could not during the course of this session extend such opportunities to the workers of British Columbia and other provinces to enable them to see their families more often, and grant them some relief by way of a greater deduction if in the course of their employment they have to maintain, as so many do in British Columbia, two homes and not just one.

Mr. Chairman, on this very subject I recall very well the minister introducing his views on, I think, December 6, 1957 as to the entitlement of construction workers to income tax exemption for expenses while away from home. It may be a coincidence, or just the income tax season, but within the last week I have received two letters from constituents who feel that this thing is not working out as expected, and I hope the minister, who I think has some sincere desire to be helpful in this matter, will really give it a look, because I think he will be impressed by the kind of letters I have received. One reads in this way:
Mr. Diefenbaker, when making his pre-election campaign speeches, made a statement to the effect that effective January 1, 1958, board and lodging paid by men living away from home working on construction jobs would be deductible for income tax purposes. With having tried this deduction before only to have it disallowed, I was very pleased that this one idea had been brought into being.
My husband had been working for the Ontario hydro in the construction division until being laid off last October. He was working away from home.
He received his T4 slips-
Then the writer of the letter goes on to quote from a hydroelectric bulletin sent to employees referring to section 23 with respect to board and lodging receipts, and so on, and there is an inference that the employee must be a householder. But she is disillusioned; the claim for deduction has been denied.
Mr. Chairman, I had another letter, as it happens in the same mail, which reads in part as follows:
I work in the construction trade and am away from my home a great deal of the time. We are required to pay for board and lodgings when away, which is in effect supporting two homes, since I have a wife and family living in Kenora.
Now, my question is this: should not the amount of money deducted from a man's wages for board and lodgings-
In accordance with the intention of the government-
-be deductible by him on his income for tax purposes?
As I say, it may be the season, but it is significant that something is going wrong with the administration. I will be very pleased to pass these letters to the minister, but I think all the fanfare that was made with respect to these matters indicates something should be done. The Ontario hydro has taken great pains to publicize this new concession with respect to tax laws, and these people now find that at the individual tax offices they are not getting the practical result that seemed to be indicated in the announcement of the minister in December, 1957 and in the speeches

of the Prime Minister subsequently during the 1958 election campaign.
I therefore think the matter should be looked into. The other night the minister gave us some advice about the difficulties of the finance minister when he is confronted with discrimination, and he mentioned the possibility that in doing something in one direction he may set a precedent and be obliged to do it in others. This was part of the difficulty that faced the former administration, and I am acquainted with that. None the less the minister advertised his intended generosity to the high heavens in this respect, and it just so happened that within two weeks I have had these two letters from constituents who say that in actual practical experience it does not seem to be working out to their advantage and in accordance with expectations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman will agree that never at any time did we make any promise or hold out any assurance or representation that we would go beyond the case of the construction worker.

These were both letters, I might add, from construction workers. I have not burdened the minister by reading the extract from the official publication of the Ontario hydroelectric commission after the minister made this decision, but I could. It is in the letter which I indicated I would send to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if reference is had to what I said on December 6, 1957 as reported at pages 2004 and 2005 of Hansard, it is made quite clear there that we were referring to construction workers and construction workers only. The language of the clause that was introduced to carry out the proposal then announced is restrictive in terms. It applies only to the man who has a spouse or a person dependent upon him by blood relationship, marriage or adoption, and who has that self-contained domestic establishment from which his work separates him.
The passages that the hon. member has read from the two letters he has received give no inkling whatever as to the grounds upon which the claim in each case may have been disallowed, but if the hon. gentleman agrees to send the letters we will be glad to make inquiries through the Department of National Revenue to ascertain the grounds upon which it was found that in those particular cases the individuals concerned did not qualify under the terms of section 5, subsection 2 of the Income Tax Act.

At least one of the writers, Mr. Chairman, has taken the pains to look up the statutes. I have not burdened the committee by reading the letter in full but
Income Tax Act
in that letter she has outlined the point that my hon. friend raises; that is, the necessity of there being a householder. In addition, she also outlines that the people for whom she speaks-not only her husband but others- were working in the construction division of the Ontario hydro and have been denied this year the out of town expenses which they thought they would be allowed as a result of the much advertised change made by the minister in December, 1957.

Mr. Chairman, I hope I may be permitted to ask a question of the Minister of Finance concerning a problem that came to my attention for the first time two or three weeks ago and about which I did not know before. I raise it at this time because we are dealing with the Income Tax Act and this has bothered me for the past few weeks.
The minister as a member of parliament and a man of the world knows that it sometimes happens that a man may be sentenced to prison for life or a person may be insane for life. Under Canadian divorce laws the husband or wife of such a person cannot obtain a divorce in order to live a normal life and it sometimes happens that they become involved in what is known as a common law way of living with a person to whom they are not or cannot be married due to circumstances beyond their control. As far as my knowledge goes a common law wife is recognized in most circumstances under provincial laws. As a matter of fact, I do not know of any law in British Columbia under which a common law wife is not recognized. I do not, of course, mean a common law wife of a few weeks or months; I refer to a common law arrangement over a period of years as a result of which there are children.
I may have been abysmally lacking in knowledge of the federal law but it was not until two weeks ago that I became aware that a common law spouse is not recognized as a dependent of the breadwinner under the Income Tax Act. I believe this places a heavy and unnecessary burden on the person who seeks to live a normal life and for reasons that are perhaps totally beyond his or her control and they enter into a common law arrangement. Under the Income Tax Act he is charged as a single person although he may have lived for years as a married person.
Such a case came to my attention. The Department of National Revenue is seeking back taxation for a period of six years against an individual who has maintained a home with his common law wife throughout that period. The department claims that he filed

Income Tax Act
a false return over the years in claiming as a dependent the woman with whom he has lived for six years. He is a working man and is now being hit very hard taxation wise.
I raised this matter in the select standing committee of this house and was told that it is a matter of law. Law relating to income tax is not decided by the Minister of National Revenue but by the Minister of Finance. I should like to ask the minister if it is not possible to recognize common law wives as dependents in reasonable circumstances for income tax purposes. Nearly all provinces recognize common law situations under certain circumstances.
Because I know how some people like to twist things I want to make it clear that I am not advocating common law arrangements but as mature adults we must recognize that these arrangements appear reasonable for those seeking a normal way of life under certain circumstances. Through you, Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister if it is not possible to give some consideration to this matter. I appreciate that the minister has to deal with important principles in the main but the height and strength of a good man is sometimes measured by his sympathetic attention to minorities and difficult problems. Is there any possible way of some provision being made in relation to the matter which I now draw to the minister's attention?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when the Income Tax Act refers to marriage or spouses or husbands or wives it refers to those who have that quality under the law. This statute does not take account of any illicit relationships in that regard. In the case of children, of course, an illegitimate child could qualify as a dependent under this act, but in the case of the woman in such a relationship she could not be treated as a wife for the purposes of this act. The hon. gentleman asks if this could be changed. Yes, parliament could change it, but that is not proposed.

I quite understand what the minister says but I do not think he would like the idea to go about that the people involved in these arrangements really wish to live outside the law. I believe the minister knows there are many people in Canada who because of circumstances have to live in a certain way in order to achieve a reasonably normal life. Sometimes I think they are more moral than those who live within the law. If the Income Tax Act is drawn in such a way that it views as illicit anyone who is not married within the law and excludes them from deductibility in terms of income tax, I should like to hear what the Minister

of Finance would say concerning all the provincial laws which recognize the status of people of good morality who are required to live outside the law.

The minister is jumping back and forth between what he classified as illicit arrangements and what I classify as necessary tax arrangements. Earlier I raised a problem about a tax deduction for transportation, board and lodging and the maintenance of two homes and the special protective clothing required by some working men. Could the minister give us an indication of what studies have been made in this respect, how extensive the studies have been and if there is an agency in his department that has studied this question would he tell us the name of the agency? I should also like to know if he is aware of any other studies that have been made and when we might reasonably expect to have a more clear and definite answer regarding the possibility of instituting such taxation deduction arrangements as those to which I referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I cannot give any indication to the hon. gentleman as to when, if ever, some proposal may be brought forward in this respect. That would not be proper with respect to any possibility of future tax policy. So far as the question is concerned, we have had some representations, but I must say not very many and not recently, on the subject. Where those representations have been received they have been reviewed to see if there was any new material in them. So far as the application of the present section is concerned as applied to construction workers, of course the Department of National Revenue is gaining more experience all the time with the application of that section and the problems of administration that arise in connection with it.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister whether any consideration has been given to the exemption of municipal property tax? The minister will recall that some members of the government side when they were in opposition, I think including His Honour the Speaker, advocated that very thing when they sat on this side. I am just wondering whether the minister has given any consideration to such a proposal, or if he will consider it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That proposal has been made from time to time over the years, Mr. Chairman. Naturally, all these proposals are reviewed from time to time, but we have not seen fit to bring forward to the house any proposal on the subject.
Pararaph 1 agreed to.

On paragraph 2.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Welland had something to raise on this paragraph.

Mr. Chairman, the corporation income tax is increased by two percentage points, and when you add this increase to the increase of one per cent on the old age pension fund you have a very high corporation tax indeed. My colleagues have put on the record-I think it was the other night-information which shows that these taxes, along with the sales tax, tend to increase the price of production and the cost of living. We have already had evidence of the increase in the cost of living. I know it is always easy to shove extra taxes on corporations because their voices are relatively few. In our free enterprise system we should not tax them out of existence. Every action or tax on the corporation tends to increase the cost of production, and certainly we know now that our production costs in this country are very high and we cannot compete in many competitive markets of the world. In fact, we find that we cannot compete in many instances in our own market. This puts many men out of jobs.
It takes some thousands of dollars in investment to put one man at work at a steady job, and unless we leave our corporations with some money for expansion I would like to ask the minister who is going to invest money to give our unemployed work? Certainly not any program of the government like the winter works program!
The talk and actions of this government have not made a climate favourable for foreign investment and particularly United States investment. Therefore, there is nothing left for us to do but to encourage our industries and to have healthy industries which will produce more jobs with security. I know that our government has about a 50 per cent interest in the earnings of our companies and corporations but it has no interest in any of the liabilities. We note that the other day it was announced that the minister had lost $10 million of the unemployment insurance account by selling bonds at a loss. I predict that the Unemployment Insurance Act will be amended-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Order. Surely, Mr. Chairman, we are not going to go into a discussion of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The committee knows very well that legislation will be introduced on this subject shortly, and surely it is highly improper now to anticipate discussion on the resolution to precede amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.

I will leave that act, except to say that I imagine industry and working
Income Tax Act
men will be called upon to pick up that $10 million, as well as many others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a resolution on the order paper.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I advise the hon. member that he is out of order.

I realize that in the past industry has exploited labour but most industrial heads that I know in my part of the country have good labour relations, and they take an interest in the labouring man. I have often got the impression from speeches in this house-and certainly I am not referring only to the government members but to some members on this side as well-that big corporations are something like an octopus; they hold back the development of our country in some ways. Our big corporations pay very high local taxes and high provincial taxes, and certainly they are now paying the highest federal tax. Contrary to the opinion held by many people, many of their shareholders are small shareholders. If you take the Bell Telephone Company, for instance, some shareholders have as low as 25 shares and others as low as 10 shares. I am not taking the part of the corporations here, but in order to save ourselves I think we must help them; we must promote their welfare so that they in turn can provide jobs with the money they make and invest in expansion of their plants.
I think the minister in this resolution is just going in the opposite direction. Our corporations should be left as much money as we can leave them under our tax structure. The minister is taxing them at the highest rate and is leaving a heavy cloud over their heads because they will have to assume their share of the $400 million which is being borrowed and carried as a deficit to be paid in future years. Also, when they borrow money to carry on their operations they must pay more because of the fiscal policy of this government. We know that this government paid 6.6 per cent net to the corporations when they bought their bonds; therefore, industry has to pay a lot-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely, we had a decision made by the house on interest rates last Tuesday night. We do not have to have it debated all the rest of the session, surely.
I will close, Mr. Chairman, by saying I regret that it has come to the time when the farmer and the grocer can go to the bank and borrow money cheaper than the Dominion of Canada can.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there any further discussion on paragraph 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should just like to correct the hon. gentleman on two of the

Income Tax Act
many erroneous statements he has made. He intimated that foreign capital was not coming into Canada. I would like to remind him that in the year 1958 foreign capital did enter Canada to the extent of $1,112 million. He is also completely wrong in the statement he made earlier that the corporation tax rate now proposed in the present resolution is the highest ever. The highest ever was in 1952 under the previous administration when the rate was 52 per cent.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I rise on a point of order. The minister has been rising repeatedly to interrupt the hon. member for Welland. When the hon. member rises on a point of order he keeps on repeating exactly what he said before. I think in fairness to the hon. member, when he is on his feet and raises a point of order at least he should be listened to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not hear or see the hon. member rising on a point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He rose twice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He did not make himself heard in my hearing on a point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is quite clear what he was doing and he was heard in this area.
I said "in recent peacetime history"; at least, I hope I said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The year 1952 was recent history and it was peacetime history and that was the year when the corporation rate was the highest, and it was not under the present administration.
Does the hon. gentleman forget Korea?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let us get the facts straight. The proposal now to raise the rate on corporation income is not the highest in history.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance pretends to correct the record. Let the Minister of Finance be reminded that in 1952 this country was engaged in an operation that most people called the Korean war. The hon. member for Welland said "in peacetime history" and what the hon. member for Welland said was perfectly correct.

Mr. Chairman, for purposes of clarification, because I admit my mind is not clear on this matter of the increase in corporation taxes, does it bear any relationship to the dominion-provincial taxation agreements? Does it have any effect on the special sections? What I have in mind particularly is the logging tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer is in the negative. This does not affect the logging tax. There is no further differential created in any respect.
Is there no special arrangement on the five-ten basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, this has no effect whatever on the provisions of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act as to the division of the yield from the corporation income tax or the right of tax abatement in the case of provinces which choose to levy their own corporation taxes.
Paragraph 2 agreed to.
On paragraph 3.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I must say that when I listened to the budget debate, if it is still proper to refer to the budget debate in the presence of the Minister of Finance, I thought that the provision the minister suggested was not unreasonable, but I have been thinking about it a bit since and it does seem to me that in most of these hospital schemes, including the one in this province, the participants pay a premium. It does not seem to me that there is any difference between paying a premium to the provincial government and paying a premium to Blue Cross. It is money out of your pocket, and I fail to understand why the view should be taken, if the service provided is contributed to in any way by the taxes paid by taxpayers on levies that are imposed by this parliament, that these expenditures should not be counted as medical expenses whereas those people who can afford semi-private or private service, which they get as a result of having paid premiums rather than paying directly, continue to get exemption.
I must say that on further reflection I am very far indeed from being convinced that this is in any way an equitable provision. Moreover, as we all know, the means of financing these hospital schemes vary greatly from province to province, and it does seem to me that the minister should give us a fuller explanation of his reasons than has been given up to now. I am not saying I am opposing this. I am saying I am worried about the equity of it and I think we ought to have a further explanation from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I gave the reasons for this in the budget speech at page 2421. It is easy enough for the hon. member to pick out the province of Ontario and say that in this province the provincial share of the cost of hospital insurance is contributed by an individual's premium and therefore it is

ascertainable and there is a receipt which can be produced. But we have to have a rule here capable of general and equitable application in all provinces. There are provinces where the provincial share of the cost of hospital insurance is not provided by way of a personal premium. For instance, in British Columbia and Nova Scotia the plan is financed by a sales tax and there is no possibility of isolating for the individual the portion of the tax he pays that is attributable to the cost in his case of the hospital insurance. Therefore, to have an equitable rule capable of application in all provinces we come forward with this proposal.
We examined this whole situation very carefully and because of the diversity of ways in which the financing of the provincial share of the cost of hospital insurance is approached in different provinces the proposal here contained is the only one that was found to be capable of general application on an equitable basis.

I do not think it has general application. That is precisely my point. Even in the province of Ontario if I apprehend the provincial law correctly-I may not but I think I do-hospital insurance is not universal. That means that those persons who are not covered by hospital insurance and who still are subscribers to Blue Cross will be able to count their hospital expenses and the rest of the people who pay a premium to the province will not. If I am wrong about that, I am wrong. I do not pretend to know all the intricacies of all provincial laws. Moreover, I imagine that in some of the provinces this is an even more generalized provision. I can see that the minister might have provided, although I think it would have worked some hardships, that in the case of general ward care or its equivalent the cost should not be deductible but it does not seem to me that the fact that you belong to a private scheme should make it possible for you to deduct and the fact that you come under a public scheme should not because those people who belong to private schemes are still treated in hospitals to which the federal government in most cases makes or has made a contribution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The situation is clear. What is proposed in this paragraph is that the taxpayer should not be entitled to have the benefit twice. In other words, to the extent that his hospital bill is paid by this scheme of public insurance to which the federal government has contributed he may not claim that portion of his hospital expense for inclusion among his medical expenses to be deducted from his income if in excess of 3 per cent of his income.
Income Tax Act
Never has it been the rule that premiums could be deducted. The only deduction ever permitted was the hospital bill.
Quite. I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Department of National Revenue did permit the deduction of the hospital bill that may have been paid by a private insurance company or some other form of insurance coverage. To the extent to which a hospital bill is not paid by or under a scheme of hospital insurance to which the federal government is contributing-obviously that is one under the act-then the individual who is charged still has a right to claim as a deductible medical expense the balance of his hospital account. There is nothing here that takes anything from him in that respect.

I do not think the minister has understood my point at all. I did not say or suggest that the premium should de deducted. I say if you pay a premium to Blue Cross or to some private company-I presume Blue Cross is not involved in this any more so perhaps I should say the Metropolitan Life or some other company that does give this kind of insurance-rather than coming under the Ontario hospital scheme, then if you have a hospital bill you can deduct the whole hospital bill although you may go to the Toronto General hospital and get exactly the same benefit as if you were under the federal scheme. That is precisely the point that I say is inequitable. If the minister will tell me my facts are wrong I will be very quickly convinced but if my facts are right, if my premise is right, the conclusion is that one person has the right to deduct his whole hospital bill and the other person has not. As I say, it seems to me that in these circumstances it is not fair in those provinces where the scheme is not universal. That is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Again I must say that the rule is quite clear. In a province where the scheme is not universal because it is not compulsory the individual who stays outside the scheme and pays his full hospital bill may deduct that full hospital bill just as an individual may in the province of Quebec, a province which thus far has not entered into the national scheme.

That is the very point; 1 am glad the Minister of Finance got to it. I, too, have been very much disturbed after reading this paragraph 3. The more I have studied it, the more disturbed I have become, and I think the Minister of Finance, a few

Income Tax Act
minutes ago, actually proved that this provision is discriminatory. Paragraph 3 of the resolution reads:
That commencing January i, 1959 the definition of medical expenses exclude those amounts which the taxpayer is not required to pay because they are paid with the assistance of the government of Canada under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.
The Minister of Finance has made what I consider to be two very important admissions. He says that after a great deal of study and consideration this proposal we now have before us was the only way in which there could be fairness under the Income Tax Act in connection with the deductibility of hospital costs. I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that is not correct. We now have in the majority of the ten provinces a national hospitalization plan under which a certain contribution is paid by the federal government on a varying basis. There are at least two provinces in which there is no such plan. In view of this, the only basis of fairness is to allow deductibility under the Income Tax Act for all hospital costs, whether the person is under one plan or another.
However, I think the major point is that which was mentioned by the minister when he sat down just a minute ago. As I understood him, he made it clear that in the province of Quebec, where there is no contractual arrangement between the federal government and the provincial government, anyone who goes into hospital will be entitled to deduct all their hospital costs for income tax purposes.
However, under paragraph 3, this will not apply to the province of British Columbia because the federal government is paying, if I am correct, 40 per cent of the hospital costs. The people of British Columbia are paying indirectly the entire cost, but directly they are paying 60 per cent of the cost. They are paying directly 60 per cent because the federal government is only paying 40 per cent. No provision is being made, in this proposal, for the people who go into hospital in British Columbia whereby they would receive any consideration for the fact that they are paying 60 per cent, although the proposal would allow 100 per cent deductibility to residents of provinces that have not entered into a contractual arrangement with the federal government under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. On the basis of the minister's own statement, therefore, this is discriminatory legislation and discriminatory taxation.
Surely, that was not basically in the mind of the Minister of Finance. I know the problems that face the minister as a result

of some provinces entering into contractual arrangements with the federal government under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. There is a difference in the way the scheme is being handled in each province. British Columbia was the second province to enter into a hospital plan. In the early days the cost of this plan was covered by the payment of premiums, but a later government adopted a two per cent sales tax to cover the cost. We now have a five per cent sales tax in British Columbia, two per cent of which is to pay for the hospitalization plan. May I point out also, that even although the province of British Columbia entered into this arrangement with the federal government, there has been no decrease in the sales tax. The people of British Columbia, therefore, are still paying the full two per cent sales tax to cover the cost of the hospitalization plan.
In addition to that, they have to pay coinsurance in British Columbia, something which I believe is not known in any other province. Even although a person is completely covered by the British Columbia plan, when you go to hospital you can be darn near unconscious but you cannot get into your room or into the operating room until you pay in advance $1 per day. I rather gathered from what the minister said that, because a person going into hospital in British Columbia has to pay this $1 per day, although he is covered by the federal and provincial plan that person can deduct this $1 per day from income tax. British Columbia being the only province that has a system of co-insurance, which means that for every day you are in hospital you have to pay $1 out of your own pocket, will that amount be deductible under income tax regulations?
As I read this amendment, that amount should be deductible. What 1 do want to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, is this:	This
amendment proposed in paragraph 3 of the resolution is discriminatory. I say that the Minister of Finance cannot get away from it because if a province has not any contractual arrangement with the federal government, then anybody going into hospital in that province is allowed to deduct 100 per cent of the hospital costs for income tax purposes. If a person in a province in which the federal government has an agreement goes to hospital, although the federal government only pays 40 to 50 per cent of the cost, that citizen cannot deduct one cent of hospital costs for income tax purposes. If the minister means what he says, that there should be no discrimination, then, difficult as the administration may be, he should allow deductibility for income tax purposes of the 40 per cent or

60 per cent of hospital costs which are not covered by the federal contribution. If that is not done, then there can be no question but that there is discrimination.
Not only is there discrimination in that regard but, in my opinion what is perhaps even of more importance, there is discrimination against the people of the province who are progressive and want to go along the line of a provincial or a federal-provincial hospital plan. This section gives aid, comfort and money to provinces which are regressive and not progressive and makes the progressive people and governments pay a penalty. Surely that is not the view of the minister who talks so much about the vision and the progressiveness of his government.
There can be no question that all the problems will not and cannot be solved until there is a complete national hospital and medical plan throughout the country. But as that matter is not coming up for consideration this year, we are obliged to consider the matter on the basis of section 3 of the present Income Tax Act resolutions. In no way, Mr. Chairman, can I see that there is no discrimination. Discrimination is there. Surely the money in any amount paid as a cost of hospitalization, whether it is a private contribution, a premium contribution or a sales tax contribution within or without a federal-dominion arrangement, should enable the payee to have the hospital bill considered as deductible under the Income Tax Act.
May I also add there something which I think we all know, namely that hospital bills are not the only ones incurred when one is ill. There are other medical bills. If there ever is a time when a person needs help, it is when he is in ill health. Medical bills can actually break a person. Surely we can give them a financial break on a hospital basis and maintain the old system of deductibility-on the present basis there is discrimination and you cannot get away from it- until such time as this government or a future government has the vision and the courage to institute national-provincial medical health insurance coverage for all the people of this nation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has in effect asked the government not to amend this present budget proposal but to undertake the amendment of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. Let me, if I can, clarify the purpose of the right to deduct expenses incurred by way of medical costs. Here is a sentence I used in the budget speech as found at page 2421 of Hansard:
The exemptions granted under the Income Tax Act for medical expenses are clearly intended to
Income Tax Act
relieve the individual taxpayer who has a burden of unusual medical expenses.
Under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, under the scheme of federal contribution to the cost, the proportion that the federal government contributes of the total cost in any province varies from province to province. Surely we cannot be expected in a budget resolution to change that situation and place all provinces on an even footing. For instance, I think the highest proportion that the federal government contributes is in the case of Newfoundland which receives from the federal government substantially more than 50 per cent of the cost of the provision of hospital insurance and diagnostic services. Other provinces, such as the one from which the hon. member comes and Ontario, do not receive as much as 50 per cent.
But here we are dealing with a tax resolution and the tax resolution is perfectly equitable in its application. The fact that the people of any particular province as a whole choose to have a greater social benefit is, in my respectful submission, no argument that they should be entitled to claim an income tax benefit when they collect the social benefit. Here we are dealing with a situation created by a federal statute and the method here proposed is an equitable proposal in dealing with the tax problem with which we are now confronted.
May I ask a question there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
