I am speaking of my own province. In view of the fact that in British Columbia the federal government will be contributing 40 per cent, can a person going into hospital in British Columbia claim 60 per cent of his hospital costs as a reduction from income tax-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
-because you are paying only 40 per cent of the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
They lose everything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The fact that the federal government makes a contribution to that particular hospital bill under the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act will, under this proposal, have the effect of eliminating that particular hospital account from the deductible medical expenses.

I want to join with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Vancouver East in protesting strongly against the inclusion of this

Income Tax Act
amendment in the Income Tax Act. The province of New Brunswick will be directly-affected by the amendment. In fact, in order to cover the province's share of the hospital insurance scheme, the citizens of New Brunswick will be obliged to pay $50 per year per family and those who want to retain the supplementary hospital benefits to cover the semi-private rate under the Blue Cross system will be obliged to pay another $30 a year, making a total of $80. Under the old plan before the hospital insurance scheme came into effect, or as it is now until July 1 when the hospital insurance scheme will come into effect in New Brunswick, under the Blue Cross system a family pays a total of $72 a year, which is $8 less than they will be obliged to pay when the hospital insurance scheme comes into force. Under the present scheme they are allowed to deduct medical expenses exceeding three per cent of their net salary, an advantage which they will not have under the new system.
Notwithstanding what the minister has just said, I assert that this amendment is an injustice to the taxpayers of New Brunswick. It deprives them of a privilege which they now enjoy under the present system. If the minister wants to be logical and if he still wants to insist that the share paid by the federal government should not be deductible, the residents of New Brunswick should at least be allowed to deduct 50 per cent of their medical expenses over and above the three per cent of their net salary, which would be the same as they are at present allowed under the Blue Cross system. The present amendment, if accepted, will create an additional burden for a large percentage of the taxpayers of New Brunswick. Again I wish to protest against this amendment. I think it should be withdrawn or at least amended in order to affect only the federal share of the amount paid to hospitals and be in agreement with the arguments advanced by the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the difficulty the department has in dealing with paragraph 3. It is pretty hard to see how the department can treat people fairly in all provinces when they pay different premiums. I think the minister announced a while ago, if I understood him rightly, that premiums were not deductible. For example, in Ontario we have to pay a premium, and I would like to ask one question at this point. Supposing a person in Ontario took out an insurance policy for which he paid a premium of $50, the approximate amount he has to pay in this participating scheme. If he had a bill of $200, would he be able to
[Mr. Robichaud.l
deduct it? If it was taken over, he would not be able to deduct it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the deductibility, where it applies, applies only to the hospital account not to the premium. It has never applied to the premium. If the hospital account is one to which the federal government makes no contributions under the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, then of course that hospital account is deductible in full as a deductible medical expense. On the other hand, if it is an account which is paid under the provisions of that act, then it will not be deductible.
As to the point raised by the hon. member for Gloucester, I think it is well to keep a sense of proportion in these matters. The federal government this year is putting up no less than $160 million as its share of the cost under the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. This present resolution will take away from the taxpayers this year the right to make deductions which are estimated to be worth to them $3 million; or in a full year, to be worth $9 million. As I say, we must keep a sense of proportion in relation to the situation before we look at this resolution out of all context and perspective.
When the hon. member for Gloucester speaks-
Could I ask a question at this point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I may be permitted to finish first. When the hon. member for Gloucester speaks about the people of his province of New Brunswick being entitled to deduct their hospital premium, I might point out that the people in the adjoining province of Nova Scotia do not pay an individual premium but are obliged to pay a provincial sales tax in order to provide the means of financing the provincial share of the hospital insurance in that province. If the hon. member remembers that he will realize that the scheme we put forward in the present resolution is the only one which is capable of equitable application to all the provinces.

Mr. Chairman, may I now ask a question. In view of the fact that under paragraph 3 we are dealing with the ill health of people, which means heavy financial responsibilities, could I ask the minister why he deems it necessary to make the scheme retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, you have to have a starting point, and January 1 is the logical starting point. Otherwise you have a broken period during the year. You would

have a year for medical expense deductions different from the year in respect of which you calculate the income.
Then how does the minister explain that in certain other cases which he has in mind he is starting them in July and not in January?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case of commodity taxes they always become effective at midnight on budget night. In the case of income taxes, normally a convenient date is selected, as for instance January 1 or July 1. In the case of some of these income taxes we have made them effective July 1, in other cases January I.
In view of the fact that the minister is making some effective July 1, as much as I oppose the entire principle here, is there any reason why this one should not be July 1?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this tax applies to the individual, and for the individual the tax year is always the calendar year. Therefore it is only proper that this provision should apply from January 1. We are not going back to 1958. That might have been proposed, but we are proposing rather to start on January 1.
How about January 1, 1960?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then you would be carrying on a discriminatory and quite unworkable situation, because in some provinces you have the situation which I talked about where the provincial share is paid by means of a sales tax. In other cases the provincial share is paid by an individual premium, and as the national system of hospital insurance came into effect for most provinces during various periods in 1958, I think it is clear that the convenient, appropriate and proper date to bring this change into effect with justice to all provinces concerned is January 1, 1959.

Is the minister aware that in the province of New Brunswick after July 1 the residents will have automatically to drop the Blue Cross scheme and will be called upon to pay $8 more than they were paying before this scheme came into effect, and this notwithstanding the contribution of $160 million from the federal government? So it is certainly of no benefit to the residents of New Brunswick who were contributing to the Blue Cross scheme.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does that conclude discussion on paragraph 3?

Mr. Chairman, I know the Minister of Finance gets as tired as I do about referring to some of our back debates, but the minister was always one who had some doubt as to the merit of even having 66968-9-209
Income Tax Act
in our income tax this 3 per cent saving clause. We apparently will continue to have it, but under new circumstances. I suggest to the minister that perhaps he should look back upon his former pronouncements advocating the elimination of this so-called floor. I am not going to put it on Hansard today but I would like to direct his attention to what he had to say on August 6, 1956 in this regard, where he advocated the elimination of the 3 per cent provision, and also felt that a greater number of particular drug items should be considered by the income tax administration with regard to income tax deductions.
Mr. Chairman, the thing which prompts me to draw this to the attention of the minister at the moment is that I think we should all recognize that if in a majority of cases the actual cost of hospitalization itself is no longer to be regarded as a portion of this over-all cost to the taxpayer on medical expense, perhaps the minister should take a further look at his ideas to the end that with regard to the items of entitlement he should be more generous than he has been hitherto.
I welcome the next paragraph and I do not wish to intrude on the rules by referring to it in detail. May I point out, however, that some items are being added to that restricted list that are entitled to consideration in the matter of an expenditure for health purposes by a taxpayer. If the actual cost of hospitalization is to be disregarded I suggest that this perhaps might reinforce the argument the minister himself used on this side of the house some years ago to the effect that there should not be any restriction at all with respect to the total of medical bills.
When we add under circumstances such as are being advanced to us now the elimination of something very big affecting nearly all taxpayers on the one hand, and then add something applicable to the odd individual such as is the case in the next paragraph, important though it may be, I think we are not arriving at a solution that is realistic. I suggest to the minister that he should have another look to see whether or not the premiums themselves should not be an item that is regarded as a tax deduction in aggregate.
I suggest that the floor of 3 per cent, or whatever it is called, should have another look taken at it. The minister always advocated this over the years. There is all the more reason for doing it if hospital bills are to be disregarded because they are the major item in the calculation of a taxpayer's expenditures in this realm in a calendar year.
I wonder if the minister would care to indicate to the committee whether or not this

Income Tax Act
has been given consideration when he is disallowing the items that would be most important for perhaps 95 per cent of claimants, namely hospitalization charges in provinces which receive some form of federal government assistance in the payment of hospitalization costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like first to observe that the point raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River with regard to the 3 per cent has no bearing whatever on the question we have been discussing and which is the purpose of the resolution, namely to determine that certain hospitalization costs to which the federal government contributes under the provisions of the act that is named shall not be deductible.
Mr. Chairman, may I be permitted to ask the minister if he does not agree that in past years he voted for the elimination of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am coming to the point about the 3 per cent. I am observing in the first place, Mr. Chairman, that the point raised has nothing whatever to do with the question we have been discussing here. It has no bearing whatever on the third paragraph of this resolution or the proposal contained in it.
As to the 3 per cent I would observe this. I have not forgotten what was said in former years but in a year when it is necessary to increase the income tax it is obviously quite impossible to consider changes of the nature proposed by the hon. gentleman.
On the third point, however, I may say that we have been moving steadily last year and this year toward the enlargement of the scope of the definition of deductible medical expenses. Last year you will remember that we introduced three very substantial additions to the list of medical expenses: prescribed drugs, eye glasses and ambulance charges. Three important additions indeed were made to the list and there were included certain other aids required by disabled persons.
In the next paragraph to which I trust we will be coming shortly we are proposing a further enlargement of the definition of deductible medical expenses as applied to certain aids for persons suffering from certain disabilities.

That was just my point, Mr. Chairman. I have here Hansard of June 17, 1958, including the resolutions that the minister had in mind last year which were in a similar category, at which time there was some enlargement of the particular items

that would be considered for tax exemption in aggregate. My point was that if you take away the base which for most people would be hospital expenses, these resolutions of 1958 and the one contained in paragraph 4 to which we will be referring, really have little point or merit.

Mr. Chairman, the minister said that this paragraph had to be put in and that this change in the act had to be made to avoid discrimination. That is just nonsense. There is no discrimination at the present time. Nothing the minister has said has removed from my mind the feeling that this is introducing a discrimination between the privately insured person and the publicly insured person and I believe the minister confirmed that by his answer to the hon. member for Welland when he said the hospital bill of the privately insured person would be deductible in full and the hospital bill of the publicly insured person would not. This is purely and simply a device for getting extra revenue and it should be recognized as such. All this talk about discrimination has nothing to do with the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member was never more mistaken in his life than in his concluding remarks. This has been approached on the basis of a facing up to a problem which has arisen and which has to be settled now in view of the fact that this federal statute has now come into effect involving various dates with respect to different provinces. The decision has to be made now. It is not made as a means of increasing revenue but as a means of grappling with a problem which if not faced up to would leave a chaotic situation with different rules applicable to different provinces.

That is utter nonsense
and the minister knows it, or at least should know it. If he does not know it he should not be Minister of Finance. There was no discrimination or difficulty so long as all hospital bills could be deducted if they came within the rules. The fact that the scheme started at different times in different provinces has nothing to do with the case and the method by which it is paid for has nothing to do with the case.
Once the principle is admitted that a person can insure against this risk and still submit his hospital bill, then if one kind of insurance enables you to make a claim under the Income Tax Act and the other does not, there is discrimination. It does not matter whether you pay a 5 per cent sales tax as you do in British Columbia where you pay a great deal more for hospital insurance than in some other provinces or whether you pay

your own bills as you do in Quebec, the plain fact is there is no discrimination as between taxpayers as long as everybody everywhere in Canada is allowed to deduct his hospital bill. That is a simple, common, universal rule and that is the law now. The only possible legitimate excuse for doing this is to get more revenue and if it gets no more revenue I think the minister should drop it. I am perfectly sure, however, that it will get considerably more revenue. For the minister to get up and create all these ridiculous smokescreens that have nothing to do with the facts surrounding this situation seems to me to be an insult to the intelligence of hon. members of the committee.
Paragraph 3 agreed to.
On paragraph 4.

Mr. Chairman, I should like
to have my medical knowledge added to. Would the Minister of Finance be good enough to explain to me what iliostomy and colostomy pads are? I am sorry but I do not know what this is all about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The iliostomy and colostomy pads referred to here are pads used in the course of post-operative treatment particularly in cancer cases.

Thank you. I should like
very sincerely to ask the minister to make a change in this paragraph. Part of the paragraph reads: "-and rocking beds for poliomyelitis patients be included". I want to assure the Minister of Finance that those rocking beds are most certainly of great value to those who suffer from poliomyelitis; but because of my interest in these matters I can assure him from my own personal knowledge in British Columbia, and in Ontario, that rocking beds have a most useful therapeutic value and are perhaps used more by those who suffer from rheumatoid arthritis and rheumatic and arthritic conditions. I am sorry that our doctor member from Welland and others are not in the committee at the moment. It is my opinion that these rocking beds are used more by those who have rheumatic and arthritic conditions than they are by those who suffer from poliomyelitis.
I rise, not so much because of my own study of this matter but in the past few years I have had the matter brought very much to my attention. The therapeutic value of the rocking bed to those who suffer from arthritic conditions, and especially rheumatoid arthritis, is a wonderful medical advance which has been made in recent years. I ask the Minister of Finance whether he would bring in an amendment and not restrict the deductibility of the cost of those 66968-9-209J
Income Tax Act
beds. I know that they are expensive and I would ask that he extend the deductibility beyond those who suffer from poliomyelitis and add it to those who have rheumatoid arthritis or something of that serious nature. I hope the minister will take it into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to be quite sure that the hon. member is actually referring to rocking beds and not to vibrators in various forms. I know vibrators are used in connection with the treatment of certain forms of arthritis; but when this resolution was drafted our understanding was that the rocking bed was used as an ancillary to the iron lung as a means of assisting the breathing of the poliomyelitis sufferer and that is the reason it appears in this form. We can look into it and see whether the rocking bed is used for other patients but our understanding when this provision was drafted was that the rocking bed was used, as I said, for poliomyelitis patients and those alone.
No sir.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We can look into it, Mr. Chairman, before the bill is introduced.

I was using the rocking bed as a layman's term. I was not referring to it in connection with the iron lung. I was referring to an actual complete bed which is now available in Canada and also in the United States about which I myself know a great deal. The layman's term is a rocking bed, because it is a full length, stretch out bed. You may call it a vibrator if you like; I do not care what you call it. All I ask is that the minister take it under advisement and include it as an exemption under the Income Tax Act, because I am certain that it is going to come more and more into use and it is going to help more and more those people who suffer from arthritis. I know, sir. My mother died just a few weeks ago and I know what this kind of thing means to many arthritics. They are expensive. I would ask that consideration be given to including it in the deductions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have already indicated we will have a look at this before the bill is introduced.

Mr. Chairman, I want to commend the department and the minister on adding these five or six further items which are deductible for income tax purposes. I should also like to draw the attention of the department to something else which I think could be included in this same group. As you know, sir, such a medication or preparation

Income Tax Act
as insulin for years has been a deductible product and it still is. Of course, along with insulin a diabetic has to use certain other types of medication, shall I say, or testing apparatus. They have to use this in the control of the disease. I am speaking particularly of testing tablets and testing tapes which are used for the purpose and actually have to be purchased by a diabetic. When they come into my pharmacy they cannot understand why I can give them a receipt for the insulin but I cannot give them a receipt for those testing tapes or testing tablets which they have to use every day in urinalysis tests for testing the albumen as it is deposited. They also have to use a hypodermic needle in the administration of insulin, which they feel should also be deductible. They also go so far as to say that the dietary scale which they have to use to measure their portions of food possibly to even up their intake and also to help in the control of this disease should be deductible. I feel that these people are worthy of consideration because of the types of medication or testing apparatus they have to use. I think I can speak from knowledge. If there were any hon. gentlemen in the house who are members of the medical profession I think they would agree most wholeheartedly with what I have to say. Any preparations along this line, Mr. Chairman; I can think of two-possibly there are more-at the present time, two types of tablets which are prescribed by the medical profession for beginners who may eventually become diabetics. You might say that the beginners are diabetics. The tablets to which I refer, and which are being prescribed by the medical profession to patients who come to me, are called orinase and mobenal. Both appear in tablet form and are taken by mouth.
I can give an insulin user a receipt for income tax deductions but I cannot give a receipt to the users of those tablets for income tax purposes, because the act specifies insulin and insulin alone. I would ask the minister to consider this because I feel it is necessary. The people who take these tablets may eventually have to go on to insulin but at the present time they are helped by the use of these tablets. I bring this to the attention of the minister. I feel it could be easily added or the act could be changed so that the testing apparatus for the diabetic and also the new tablets which are being prescribed could be deducted.

May I add a word to that? I am glad that a member of the pharmacy profession has raised this because I have also been asked by citizens from Vancouver to raise the identical matter. Medical science

progresses but unfortunately costs in many instances do not come down. There is a trend now from using a needle to taking the medicine orally but it is still very expensive. The diabetic still has to have his dosage whether he gets it by needle or by mouth. I want to add my voice to what has been said by the member who just spoke. Why does the Income Tax Act say that if you take the drug by needle the expense can be deducted but if you take it by mouth, even though it is for the same purpose, it is not deductible? The whole attitude is completely ridiculous and asinine and I hope the minister will bring in the required change. I am certain, as the hon. member has just said and as every medical man will say, that it is a logical and reasonable request.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The remarks of the hon. members have been noted and, of course, these subjects are being studied from year to year. I do point out, however, that with respect to hypodermic needles or some of the other means of administering insulin or other medicaments hon. members will require to bear in mind that these needles are capable of use for other purposes as well quite outside the purposes of this section, and care must be taken in these respects not to introduce into the definition of medical expenses various medical appliances that are capable of other uses.

I am very sorry that the Minister of Finance spoke in that way because the remarks made by the previous speaker and myself dealt wholly and solely with diabetics. Prescriptions for diabetes must be obtained from a doctor whether the medicine is to be administered by a needle or taken orally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it is a doctor's prescription it is within the scope of the definition now, but we have had representations respecting the inclusion of needles and means of administering hypodermic injections and there we have been up against the situation that such appliances are capable of other uses as well. We are considering these matters all the time.
It takes so long.

Objection has been taken to hypodermic needles and I agree with the minister that we sell them for many other purposes as well. But I should like him to consider particularly the testing that is necessary for the diabetic. Without having a test he does not know what is the proper amount of insulin to take. The other point I should like to emphasize has to do with these tablets taken by mouth. They are not deductible

because the act refers to insulin but while they are not insulin they are used for the same disease.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That will be looked into.
Paragraph 4 agreed to.
On paragraph 5.

I think perhaps it would help us if the minister would amplify his intentions with respect to this paragraph. I know that there will be details in the bill but the language of the bill is always very complicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Paragraph five of the present resolution provides that in future an individual will not be required to include in his income any lump sum that he receives out of an employees' pension plan upon severance of employment to the extent that he uses that lump sum payment within the year or within sixty days after the end of the year as a contribution into a new pension plan or as a premium under a registered retirement savings plan. If an employee leaves his employment where he has been a member of a pension plan he usually receives a lump sum representing the return of his contributions into the pension plan. This lump sum payment may also contain all or part of the employer's contribution into the pension plan.
Under the present law this lump sum payment is liable for tax in the year in which it is received and it is because we consider that inequitable that we are moving now in the terms of paragraph five. In those cases where the employee transfers from the pension plan of a former employer to that of a new employer and there is a direct transfer of all the funds to the credit of the employee from the former employer's pension plan to that of the new employer, the Department of National Revenue has not in practice regarded the transfer to be a payment to the employee and consequently no tax problem has arisen. But in cases where there is no direct transfer from the former employer to the new employer it is quite clear that difficulties are going to arise before very long, and that is why we are moving now to make this provision that where, in the terms of paragraph five, an amount is received out of a pension fund or plan upon withdrawal or retirement from employment or upon the winding up of the fund the individual is not required to include in income the portion of the fund that is paid in the year, or within 60 days after the end of the year, as a contribution to a registered retirement pension fund or plan or as a premium under a registered retirement savings plan. In other words, to the extent that he uses the withdrawal from the
Income Tax Act
fund within that year or within 60 days of the end of the year by putting it into a new pension plan, whether it is a pension plan under a new employer or one of the registered retirement savings plans, then that sum withdrawn is not going to be regarded as income.
That seems to have merit. In addition, has it some element designed to encourage mobility of labour with respect to pension plans and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will not say that it will encourage mobility but it will mean that an individual who wishes to change his employment will not, to the extent that he brings himself within this new provision, forfeit his tax position. As long as his contribution was in the fund he was not taxable but if on severance of employment he withdrew his share of the fund, which might include something from the employer, and it did not go directly into the new fund, he would be liable to tax on that withdrawal as the act stands today.

I must say that we most certainly welcome this change in the act as explained by the minister. We sincerely hope that this is only a first step. We trust it is an indication that the department and the government have recognized the importance of introducing new legislation with respect to portable pensions. I have no hesitation in saying that one of the next steps in the realm of security in Canada should be to deal with portable pensions because in some provinces in particular people go from one industry to another, one job to another, and as a general rule they have up till now lost all their pension rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit me to say that I am afraid this is a matter beyond federal jurisdiction. We can deal only with the question of pension rights so far as taxes are concerned, but when it comes to questions of rights of individuals in pension plans that obviously is a matter of property and civil rights and under provincial jurisdiction.

I would not deny the influence of the federal government or the Minister of Finance when, in the House of Commons at this session, he introduces an amendment to the Income Tax Act giving an indication that the transference of pension funds is a good thing. He says that under certain circumstances, as Minister of Finance, he is not going to include it for income tax purposes, and this will help a person build up his own future security. I think it is a good rule. I hope it is an indication of the recognition of portable pensions. I hope that since the Minister of Finance has now made his move

Income Tax Act
the provinces will follow suit with the additional legislation required.

I wonder if the minister has any figures to show how many persons are taking advantage of that admirable provision which was made by Mr. Harris in his last budget for these retirement savings plans for the self-employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are no statistics available at the present time. It may be that some will be available by the end of the year, based upon a sampling of the 1958 returns.
Paragraph 5 agreed to.
On paragraph 6.
On No. 6, Mr. Chairman, would the minister outline to the committee what has been the practice of the administration in the absence of the proposed law?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The current practice simply conforms to the provisions of the old section 139, subsection (1) (j) (ii). This is the provision in the interpretation section of the act that is applied to death benefits, and in effect it permits payment by the employer, without income tax liability, of an amount equal to the remuneration of the officer or employee, to his widow or legal representative of a sum equivalent to his remuneration for the last 90 days in the office or employment. I think my hon. friend is familiar with this provision. It has been in the act for some time. It is the one that was inserted originally to give encouragement to the payment by employers on the death of an employee or officer of a sum not exceeding the equivalent of three months' salary or remuneration as a recognition of services rendered in the lifetime of the deceased employee.
Now this amount would be limited to $10,000, regardless-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but we are
proposing to enlarge the three months' period to twelve months. If the house approves of this proposal, we will place an over-all ceiling of $10,000 on the payment so that advantage will not be taken of this in the case of persons with very large salaries. For instance, at the present time it is possible, under this three months' provision, in the case of a senior executive of a large corporation, let us say with a salary of $100,000, to make tax free a payment of $25,000. We are proposing to enlarge this provision laterally in order to benefit more people and encourage the making of provision in proper cases by an employer for the widow or dependents of a deceased employee, up to 12

months' salary, but in doing so we think it proper to propose that a ceiling of $10,000 be placed on the total.
In other words, if the law was not to be evaded, a retired employee would have to provide evidence of departure from the business concerned-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, this applies only in the case of his death.
Paragraph 6 agreed to.
Paragraphs 7 and 8 agreed to.
On paragraph 9.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I indicated earlier there would be an amendment here. Several days ago I gave a copy of the proposed amendment to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and the hon. member for Assini-boia. I will ask my colleague the Minister of National Defence to move the amendment, which is as follows:
That paragraph 9 of the Income tax resolution be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"or in the case of corporations incorporated prior to April 10, 1959 that did not have a 1958 taxation year, that so qualify for the first fiscal period ending after 1958."
This paragraph will now read:
9. That the privilege of qualifying as a foreign business corporation be withdrawn except for those corporations that were so qualified for the 1958 taxation year or in the case of corporations incorporated prior to April 10, 1959 that did not have a 1958 taxation year, that so qualify for the first fiscal period ending after 1958.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I so move.

This particular amendment is one about which people with much more knowledge in this field than I have have expressed some surprise after reading about the minister's intention. I think we should have the fullest possible statement from him as to the advantages of the amendment. Even a week ago the Financial Post described this amendment as an enigma; they just could not understand the merits of it. I assure the committee and the minister that I am very naive in matters of this kind.
In order to explain properly to other members of the committee who may have similar difficulties to mine, all I can say is that I am familiar with such well known Canadian corporations as Brazilian Traction and some others who perform no active business in Canada but have their incorporation here in Canada. They have officers and head offices and the like in Canada, but hitherto they have not been subject to the normal rules of taxation because they are not competitive businesses in our country. The thing that has concerned me after a reading of this resolution is that corporations of this kind,

whether on a large scale or small, having their business headquarters in Canada, with personnel who perhaps have a Canadian background and which contribute something to the commercial life of this country but without competing with other Canadian corporations-I can think of accountants, lawyers and even individual employees at the head office level-have been encouraged to establish in Canada.
When I find myself in association with the Financial Post in saying that they are in complete ignorance of any reason for this kind of amendment to the law; when, on the face of it, one would have thought we had some advantages to gain and we cannot see the advantages of changing the past set-up, I think a full explanation is due the committee from the minister and I am sure he will give it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Gladly, Mr. Chairman. This resolution is designed to introduce changes in the provisions of section 71 of the act. Section 71 of the Income Tax Act provides:
71. (1) No tax is payable under this part upon the taxable income of a corporation for a taxation year when it was a foreign business corporation.
No corporation is incorporated in the first instance, whether under federal or provincial charter or letters patent, which is to begin with a foreign business corporation; but under quite detailed rules that are laid down in section 71 in its various clauses it is possible for a corporation to qualify in a tax sense as a foreign business corporation. If it does so, it obtains great tax advantages under the act. For instance, it has no corporate income in Canada subject to the normal corporation income tax here because its income is earned outside of Canada. In the ordinary case, unless this corporation pays a dividend to a non-resident corporation which controlled its stock-in which case there would be a five per cent tax deducted-there would not be any revenue accruing to the federal treasury from this particular company, expect to the extent to which it may employ a few people in its skeleton organization and some personal income tax is collected upon their salaries. But so far as the corporation is concerned, unless it pays a dividend to the parent corporation abroad, the Canadian government collects no tax from this corporation.
As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has indicated, it is quite true that there are some important and highly regarded corporations which, under the Income Tax Act, are regarded as foreign business corporations. They have qualified. But, Mr. Chairman, we are concerned lest the provisions of
Income Tax Act
section 71 should be used either to create in Canada a tax haven or as a means of tax avoidance. I am not saying that is being done at the present time but from our studies of the section and its quite detailed provisions we are concerned lest in the future advantage should be taken of certain features of the provisions of section 71 for these purposes. Therefore we have approached this matter on the basis of not taking away from any existing corporation any rights it has in this respect. We began by saying that any corporation that had qualified as a foreign business corporation up to the end of 1958 would be entitled to enjoy in the future the same benefits as it enjoyed prior to the budget as a foreign business corporation.
And you have amended it as of budget night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then the question arises as to what happens in the case of a corporation that may not have been incorporated before 1959, or may not have yet qualified in respect of its fiscal period commencing in 1958. That is the purpose of the amendment, namely to make sure that we are not taking away anything that any corporation may have acquired by way of right up to the moment of the introduction of the budget. Therefore, in the result, the resolution in amended form takes nothing away from any existing corporation which may have qualified. Second, it takes away from no existing corporation any right or opportunity that it may have to qualify in respect of the business it was doing up to the date of the introduction of the budget or the next day following. We are therefore taking nothing away from anybody. There is no retroactive operation whatever in this intended provision. By closing the class now under the existing provision we are taking what we regard as a desirable step to prevent use being made of the section in the future for either of the two purposes with which we are concerned.
Our study of the situation is not going to end with the adoption of the resolution or the bill if the committee approves it. We intend to go on studying this situation. But it is requisite, Mr. Chairman, that during this period of study we should make sure that when people are put on notice we do not have a flood of people coming in seeking to qualify in this period while the matter is under study. I think my hon. friend will agree that when we are not taking anything away from anybody, in order to permit unimpeded study of this problem to proceed the class be closed now. I again emphasize the fact that we are not taking away from any corporation anything that it

Income Tax Act
has today. We are taking nothing away from it as to its right to qualify during this period of 1959 up to April 10.

I appreciate what the minister says when he makes the point that there is nothing retroactively damaging to existing corporations in the resolution proposed. But I again come back to the point that I do not understand the merit to the crown or to the country. What harm are we trying to avoid from past practice? I see nothing but advantage in the few instances that have come to my attention. I think it is a matter of pride for most Canadians that a company like Brazilian Traction calls itself a Canadian corporation. I am not complaining about any of their policies. I am not familiar with them. We know it is a large enterprise abroad. The situation is rather the reverse of one that we sometimes complain of, namely that we have foreign corporations of too much magnitude running things in our country. It shows that Canadians are prepared to invest and take an interest everywhere in the world. I have no intimate knowledge of one or two of these illustrations, but within the last few days or so I have been told that it has been to the advantage of, shall we say, a parent Canadian oil company which has no intention of utilizing its Canadian business operations in world trade; but because of patriotism and connections, shall we say, in some of our cities and associations with lawyers, accountants and professional men expert in the oil business residing in our country, they have felt that if they were to expand it was desirable that they have a Canadian corporation that would be operating exclusively outside this country and entitled to the very thing that has built up some of these other countries. What is the advantage of that?
I have also heard about certain international trading organizations that I think we would want to encourage. We want Canadians to be internationally-minded, and so on, and I am told that some enterprising Canadians who have substantial main enterprises in Canada still, being sufficiently Canadian-minded, decided if they were going to expand their international or worldwide activity they would like to see that new corporations have a Canadian charter, even though its business would be entirely outside of this country. I am persuaded that an enterprise of that kind initiated by Canadians is of benefit to Canada. I am persuaded that it does give employment to a number of ancilliary performers at the head office level, but I just have not had from the minister, as I see it, any explanation of the deleterious effects, if any, which have

come to this country or to our tax position from the companies which admittedly are not going to be affected but which have carried on in this way with Canadian head offices in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not suggesting for a minute that any Canadian corporation that has qualified as a foreign business corporation has abused the law in any respect whatever, but I know my hon. friend would not expect me to enlarge on the subject of how this section of the act in its present form might be used by someone as a means of maintaining in Canada a tax haven or as a means of avoidance of tax. I do not wish to enlarge on that subject here at this time; I think the reason is obvious.
Our approach, therefore, is this-and this is repetition. We do not take anything away which anybody has now, but we are saying that in this forthcoming period we are blocking any possibilities of the section being put to a use that parliament may not have intended. In this period we will go further with our studies of the matter.
In the meantime I think my hon. friend will recall that there is no yield from such corporations to the federal treasury whatever. Because their business is carried on abroad in order to qualify as a foreign business corporation there is no corporate income tax payable by them to Canada.
My hon. friend put the case of a Canadian parent corporation setting up such a corporation in Canada. In that case if any dividend is paid by the subsidiary, which is the foreign business corporation, to the parent, there is no tax on the dividend. I put the other case where a foreign corporation-a parent corporation abroad-chooses to form in Canada one of these foreign' business corporations; in that case there would be a 5 per cent tax withheld for the benefit of the Canadian treasury from dividends payable by the Canadian subsidiary to the parent corporation abroad. But if it is a Canadian parent corporation forming this corporation in Canada, there would be no tax deduction at all.
Therefore, this is a very important tax concession. Any corporation can, if it qualifies as a parent business corporation under section 71, derive thereby important tax advantages, and while there may be advantages to Canada in terms of employment of a few people at head office, in many cases simply a skeleton staff and no more, we think that before we should allow this situation to continue where we have concern about the possibility of the section being used in the two ways I have indicated we should close the door now and

leave it closed until another form of legislation is introduced which will not be capable of being misused in either the two ways I have indicated.

Mr. Chairman, I am by no means satisfied. The minister indicates that anybody who so far is incorporated and given the tax arrangement that he thinks should be denied in the future has not particularly abused the situation, but the minister has given me no instance of where it has resulted in some loss to the treasury. He is now proposing to do something new. Obviously, then, any little advice which he gives to this committee about the opportunities open to these people will not affect them. He has a big majority behind him and he will probably put through this proposed change in the legislation. But I do think that without naming any companies or anything of that kind he should indicate to this committee what is the possible loophole or loss-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have tried to do that. I say that under the terms of the present act there is a possibility that it can be used as a tax haven with no benefit to Canada, and it may also be used for tax avoidance.

Taking those last few words and sticking to them, can we not correct our present statute to avoid that without saying we should not have any more Brazilian Traction companies operating in Canada, or should not have any more of the international trading companies which I have heard about out in Vancouver trying to cultivate business in an admirable way for Canada in the Far East, and things of that kind where the operation is under Canadian leadership? That in turn is giving employment at the head office level at least to a great number of Canadians. I have not any personal experience with these corporations.

I do not think we have had an explanation from the minister.

Mr. Chairman, before this paragraph passes I think someone on this side of the house will have to take some exception to the very extraordinary principle enunciated by the minister in respect to this paragraph. If I may put what he said in my own words, the minister has told us that if the law were left as it is now some dire and dreadful things might happen but that we were not competent to know what those things would be, that they are so secret they must be kept from parliament and that we would have to adopt this recommendation on faith.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not what I said.

The minister can reinterpret or tell us what he did mean when he rises to reply. If the Minister of National Defence had come in and said that his department was doing in the national research council or the defence research board some very secret research work into a very secret weapon the committee might have accepted that, but for the Minister of Finance to come in here and say that if the law is left as it is it might result in Canada becoming a tax haven or it might result in tax evasion, and then to say "but I am not going to tell you how that could happen and you will have to accept it on faith", is to propose a doctrine that I believe is quite preposterous.
It is parliament, after all, that is being asked to pass this tax legislation. Surely members of parliament are entitled to know why the minister thinks there is this dreadful danger in leaving the law as it now is. He has told us absolutely nothing, has given us no information. He said we must accept on faith; father knows best.
This all-wise government-and here I am paraphrasing things that used to be said by the hon. member for Eglinton about the former administration-this all-wise, allknowing, arrogant government knows what is going to happen in the future and we are expected to take it on faith. As I understood it, that was the gist of the minister's argument for this proposed amendment. It seems to me that is something parliament should not be asked to do at all. We should

Income Tax Act
be told why this change is proposed. After all, there could be no danger because, as my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River pointed out before dinner, the government has a large enough majority so that it is quite sure that in the end, if it insists, this resolution will be passed and therefore the law will no longer be, if the minister has his way, in the state it was before. Therefore this argument of secrecy has no validity.
It seems to me that the minister should take parliament into his confidence and give us the information on which he is asking us to change the law that seems to have done no Canadian any harm and that the minister himself admitted has done no harm in the past. I submit it is his duty to inform parliament and that the minister should explain precisely what it is that he fears and what he feels is going to be against the public interest if he wants us to agree to change this part of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have just heard a very finished demonstration of misinterpretation of what I had to say. I will go over the ground again in the hope that this time my words will be clearer to the hon. gentleman and there will be no possible danger of misinterpretation.
What I said, Mr. Chairman, was that section 71 is a quite complicated section. It has been amended by parliament in the past and the two dangers that after no little study of this question we see are that the section can be used, with no advantage to Canada, as an occasion for making Canada a tax haven for those who wish to come here and use this jurisdiction simply as a tax haven, and on the other hand that it may be used for tax evasion.
I do not think hon. members wish me to point out in this section where we see the possibility of these dangers. On the best advice available to the government and to the Minister of Finance in preparing these budget proposals there are possible loopholes in this section which might be used for these purposes. I do not think it is the wish of parliament that Canada should be used without any advantage to Canada simply as a tax haven for those who do their business abroad or that it should be used in any situation for the purpose of tax evasion. That is the situation expressed quite simply.
The resolution in the amended form that is proposed takes nothing away from any corporation that has acquired rights under it or that has in respect of the period since the first of this year found itself in circumstances where it might qualify in respect of its 1959 taxation period. Those rights remain untouched by this proposed resolution. We are

proposing, however, that the right to qualify as a foreign business corporation should not accrue hereafter to any corporation which has not already entitled itself under section 71 to be treated as a foreign business corporation or in the circumstances in which it has found itself since January 1 of this year has acquired the means of qualifying as a foreign business corporation in respect of this present taxation period.
We are asking the committee for that reason to close the door at that point because there is a very serious question as to whether any more foreign business corporations are going to be of any advantage to Canada anyway. The foreign business corporation by definition is a corporation that simply is incorporated here and carries on its business outside Canada entirely. Hon. members will observe this if they look at the provisions of section 71. Such a corporation becomes subject to no corporation tax here because it does not do any business in Canada but it enjoys the benefit of the laws of Canada and the protection of Canadian laws without paying us any revenue. We therefore think this situation is one that calls for some review and we propose that no more corporations not yet entitled to qualify as foreign business corporations should be in a position to do so hereafter until at least this whole situation has been carefully reviewed. That is the reason, Mr. Chairman, why a resolution is proposed which will if approved by the committee prevent more corporations coming into existence and acquiring these favoured rights under our income tax legislation.

Mr. Chairman, just before the dinner recess the minister indicated to the committee that from his point of view he thought he had explained to me three times the reasons for this proposal. I am no expert in this field, but during the dinner recess I made a number of inquiries among people whom I regard as having a great deal of experience in matters of this kind. They tell me that they are just as much in the dark as was the Financial Post for any explanation as to the reason for this tax change. I am told that they had the same general impression that I had, that while those corporations do not particularly pay taxes to Canada, they did seem to contribute in a broad way substantial advantages in that their head offices were in Canada. They have employees paying personal income taxes here and they could not think of a thing that was detrimental to Canada in the activities of the corporations that they were conducting.
I still have not got from the minister any indication of what loss, either in revenue, in integrity or in proper activity there is in

adherence to the law as we have had it up to now. While the minister brought up the question of some kind of security and not wanting to indicate loopholes to taxpayers either in the past or to come, he was completely disregarding the fact that every taxpayer of this kind has been protected up to this particular time and other taxpayers from this time on will be denied any right that they will regard as a loophole. What are those loopholes? What are those advantages to the foreign corporations that are disadvantages to the crown?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me give an example. Hon. members opposite wish to know the loopholes.
We want to know the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They wish to know the loopholes that we see in this legislation. Let me give you a possible case, Mr. Chairman. Let us take a situation in which natural resources of Canada are involved in export. A foreign business corporation, we will say, is set up as a selling agent in connection with the export of some Canadian natural resource. The foreign business corporation, we will say, purchases from the Canadian producer at the going price and is able to sell at a very much higher price in the country to which the goods are exported because of the particular demand for the product there.
The profit that is made is not subject to tax in Canada and it is not subject to tax in any other country. When the time comes to distribute the profits of the foreign business corporation, let us say it moves its residence outside of Canada so that no tax is payable on the distribution of the profits. If we consider that the general rule is that residents of Canada must pay Canadian income tax on their income from sources in Canada and from sources outside Canada, I put it to the committee that it is just not proper that all taxes should be avoided in this way through resort to the expedient of a foreign business corporation.
Canada has tax conventions with certain foreign countries. In some of those conventions it is provided that selling agents of Canadian corporations operating in those foreign countries shall not be subject to income tax unless there is a permanent establishment such as a selling office or the location of salesmen who have power to contract in those foreign countries. Where the selling agent is set up as a separate company it might qualify as a foreign business corporation, take advantage of the tax convention 66968-9-210i
Income Tax Act
and also be free from tax in Canada. Therefore, you see, Mr. Chairman, that here you have all the makings of a situation in which Canada becomes a tax haven and where Canada derives no benefit whatever.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asks what harm are they doing if they set up an office here and employ a skeleton staff? They may not be doing any positive harm. The fact is they are enjoying very substantial tax advantages in Canada, and we think it is better, when those corporations in the situation I have indicated do not bring any advantage to Canada, they should not enjoy a special tax advantage. It would be very much better in those cases if such corporations were here not as foreign business corporations but were here and paid taxes in Canada in the same way as other corporations and individuals do.

Mr. Chairman, I continue to plead no great knowledge of the instances of individual companies but, as I said this afternoon, we do think of a large foreign corporation in Canada with which most of us are familiar, and I think of Brazilian Traction.

Mr. Chairman, somone on this side of the house asked what my qualifications were as a witness for the purpose of answering this question. The price at which liquor sells in any province is established, of course, by the provincial liquor outlet, normally the liquor commission of the province. Mr. Chairman, the corresponding levy on spirits imported from abroad will be found in the Customs Tariff. To answer the hon. gentleman's second question, there are two kinds of duties. There are excise duties and there are customs duties. The excise duties are levied upon certain Canadian products. The customs duties are levied on certain imported products.
As the hon. gentleman knows, the Excise Act is an act which levies excise duties upon alcohol in various forms, and we will be turning to the Customs Tariff for the corresponding levies by way of customs duties on corresponding imports. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Broadly speaking, an excise duty is levied at the time that the goods pass out of some form of government control, out of bond, for example. The excise tax is the type of tax that is levied at some stage as the goods pass freely from hand to hand. For instance, the sales tax as we know is levied at the manufacturer's or producer's level. The excise duty is levied before the goods are permitted to move into circulation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am quite overwhelmed by the presentation the hon. gentleman has made of his case. It is extremely touching indeed. The fact is that we must have some additional revenue. Apparently the hon. gentleman regards taxes as a penalty, at any rate if they are levied on cigarettes. By the same token, if that reasoning is sound, I suppose any tax levied on

anything is something of a penalty. Against that argument I have to put before the hon. gentleman the view that however we may look at taxes, whether darkly or otherwise, no one has found a way of financing the services that governments must provide and are expected to provide nowadays, apart from levying taxes for the purpose.
If the hon. member thinks that we should have chosen something else, may I say that I am not aware of anything else in the way of a tax that could be said to be painless. The hon. member speaks about income tax. In the course of discussion on the budget and since then we have been told that there is nothing painless about the income tax. Hence I cannot see a distinction in kind or any fundamental difference between a tax on this particular commodity and other kinds of taxes that may be regarded as necessary for the purpose of raising revenue.
As to the extent of the levy, the proposed increase actually amounts to a bare fraction under two cents a package. With the increase in the sales tax it comes out to 2.2 cents per package. Put it on the basis of the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The rate that will be in effect now is certainly not the highest rate that has been levied on cigarettes in the past. During the war the tax on a package of 20 cigarettes reached 21.7 cents. Effective April 10, 1951, it was increased by our predecessors in office to 25.21 cents per pack. I am speaking of taxes only, the combination of excise tax, excise duty and sales tax.
I thought we were at peace and in Conservative prosperity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, we are. That is why I think the hon. member can well afford to pay one-ninth of a cent more by way of tax per cigarette. I think he will enjoy it that much more realizing that he is contributing something toward paying the cost of the substantial social security measures which this government has introduced for the benefit of the people of Canada.
The prosperity is going up in smoke.

Do the members of the
minister's own party not also smoke?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I mentioned, the total of federal tax was advanced on April 10, 1951, to 25.1 cents per pack. On April 8, 1952, a year later, it was reduced, but it remained at 22.1 cents per pack for
Excise Tax Act
another year until the eve of the 1953 election when it was reduced further to 17.7 cents per pack of 20 cigarettes, which tax has been in effect for the past six years. There we have the story, Mr. Chairman.
The tax on cigarettes or cigars is not nearly as heavy in this country as it is in some other countries. There was a time when we, when in opposition, pointed out to the government of the day, with respect to this record high tax they imposed on cigarettes, that they were putting a premium on smuggling. When the cigarette tax was at its peak it was known that there was a good deal of smuggling going on. But the situation has quite drastically changed since that time. In those days there was a wide differential between the price of a package of cigarettes in the United States and the price of a package of cigarettes in Canada. The difference was so wide that there was a great incentive to smuggle. But that gap or that differential has been greatly narrowed since that time as a result of the increase of taxes in the United States. Today the differential is so much smaller that it is not anticipated that this modest increase in the tax on Canadian cigarettes or the cigarettes sold in Canada will be any encouragement to smuggling.
In addition, there are provinces which themselves levy provincial taxes on cigarettes.
All things considered, this tax was regarded as being as painless a way of finding needed revenues as any that could be resorted to. I hope that my hon. friend, in paying one-ninth of a cent additional tax per cigarette, will derive satisfaction from the fact that he is thereby increasing the revenues that will be used for the purpose of sustaining the social security program and other measures of a kind that the people of Canada seem to desire.

I want to address a few words to the minister with respect to this problem, probably from a slightly different angle. The people in my area who are in the tobacco-growing business are quite concerned about the increase in excise tax. As the minister has indicated, they well remember the results that followed from the increase back in 1951 when the law of diminishing returns set in to the extent that growers in the area suffered a decrease in production of some three million pounds. Of course, as in any other industry, when there is a reduction in production, when you are not working at peak capacity, the result is a certain amount of inefficiency. There again the people are quite concerned lest this condition might set in again.

Excise Tax Act
To many Canadians this increase is just a statistic but to the farmers of Norfolk who grow the crop it is a threat to their maximum production. To many hon. members and people throughout Canada tobacco probably is considered a luxury. I suppose when it was completely an import product brought into Canada it was a luxury. However, today the people in my area who brought a poor sandy soil back into a condition of productivity, so that they are now able to earn a reasonable living, do not consider it a luxury at all. Neither do they consider it a luxury when they compare their income to the income the federal treasury receives from tobacco. Nor do they consider it a luxury when they consider the tremendous amount of capital investment in land and equipment and the high cost of growing an acre of tobacco, which is something over $500 an acre, and also the tedious hours of hard labour. On top of all that, we have many hazards such as wind, hail and frost which in one year can bring total disaster to a season's work.
Therefore we are vitally concerned in it from the standpoint of the economic condition of the area, not only to the farmers but to surrounding businesses as well. The question I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister is that we would like some assurance from him that the law of diminishing returns will not set in.
