Then he went on:
If the taxes were lowered on tobacco-
This is the present Minister of Transport speaking in 1957-
-more tobacco products would be sold and therefore the gross intake would be greater.
The Minister of Finance apparently does not believe this and does not agree with the economic philosophy of his colleague, the Minister of Transport.
This has been proved when some time ago the price of cigarettes was raised. You all know what happened. The sales dropped off and consequently the gross intake. The tax was lowered and up went the sales and the intake.
Then the minister went on to hold out the same hopes about automobiles, and you remember what the minister did to them.
That was not the only occasion upon which high hopes were held out, and the Minister of Transport was not the only one who held them out. On February 18, 1958 the Hamilton Spectator carried this account of a meeting the Prime Minister had at Brantford:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker blew a warm blast of optimism over this sub-zero city last night.
I imagine the news that the cigarette tax was going to be raised blew a cold blast over that optimism. I forgot to read the heading of this article, and perhaps 1 should read it for the benefit of the hon. member for Norfolk, the hon. member for Elgin, who is not here, and the hon. member for-

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The hon. member for Elgin is here.
Then I beg the hon. member's pardon; I was thinking of the hon. member for Oxford. The hon. member for Oxford is not here.
Yes he is.

Well, the hon. member for Kent, who is no doubt here and will speak for himself, and the hon. member for Essex South and the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. I am sure he is delighted with these increases in the cigarette taxes. Now, this report is only a year ago,

before the election. This is the kind of thing that the tobacco growers of this country were being treated to. This is the heading: "Optimistic Prime Minister Hints PC's Would Trim Tobacco Taxes". I imagine the average person on reading that would think by "trim" was meant taking something off. I suppose the word could be used in the opposite sense of putting more trimming on in the form of additional tax.
Trimming the taxpayers' pockets.

Yes, and also in another sense, as the hon. member for Gloucester has reminded me, of trimming the taxpayer. Perhaps that is what the Prime Minister had in mind. Here is what the Prime Minister is quoted as having said:
"The tobacco industry has asked for some action, and we are having the question looked into-"
You know the way the Prime Minister is always looking into things-
"-to ascertain what action should be taken to assist the tobacco growers to achieve fair and reasonable returns", said Mr. Diefenbaker, who is a non-smoker.
I really do not know what that has to do with the subject.
You are a non-smoker.
Yes, that is true.
Then why mention it?

The hon. member for Cape Breton South like Pontius Pilate stays not for an answer, but I will give one. I mentioned it to show how disinterested I was, because as far as my pocket is concerned it does not matter to me what the tax on cigarettes is. But I am a strong believer in governments keeping their promises and in public men carrying out their promises.
Oh, oh.

There certainly could be no more glaring example anywhere than in this particular case, because if there is one industry which was singled out both in 1957 and 1958 and told the Liberals had discriminated against it, and given the impression, as I have shown here from this article, that this government was going to do the opposite, it was the tobacco growers as the hon. member for Norfolk well knows. I understand he actually had his picture taken with the Prime Minister holding up a package of cigarettes and telling the growers of the wonderful things which would be done for them. But I will stick to the text which I have before me. I have not got the pictures here but I do have these words attributed to the Prime Minister:
Excise Tax Act
"The tobacco industry has asked for some action and we are having the question looked into to ascertain what action should be taken to assist the tobacco growers to achieve fair and reasonable return," said Mr. Diefenbaker, who is a nonsmoker.
He added:	"The tobacco industry has not
received the consideration it has deserved".
Apparently it has now got the consideration which the Minister of Finance thinks it deserves and it has got it in the form of an increase in the tax. I could go through a lot of other clippings. Apparently this hinting went on in a good many places in western Ontario during those two election campaigns, but it does not seem to me that the number of the promises, which were made outside the house and therefore would be the kind of second class promises that the Minister of National Revenue referred to the other day, makes any difference. I am sure that the hon. member for Norfolk and his constituents believed that when the Prime Minister talked about some kind of action, that kind of action was going to be the kind of action that the tobacco growers expected and not the exact opposite.
It is true that you can twist these words around and argue that the Prime Minister was really warning then that the tobacco growers and tobacco consumers were going to have to pay the cost of his extravagance. That is perhaps what he really warned them of in this rather veiled language. I am sure, however, that all the electors in the tobacco districts of Ontario, every constituency of which returned a Tory member, are going to feel pretty disillusioned about any further promises emanating from hon. gentlemen opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
cannot deny myself the pleasure of saying something in immediate succession in the course of debate to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. The carpet of the chamber is already wet in front of him with the crocodile tears that gushed forth from his eyes. This outburst has come from an hon. member as spokesman of a party which in 1951 raised the tax on cigarettes to 25.1 cents a package.
During the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under pressure
of demand from the Conservative opposition of that time that government the following year reduced the price to 22.1 cents per package. It was under pressure from the Conservative opposition of that day-

Mr. Chairman, I know
that the minister does not want to be unfair-

Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -that the Liberal party then proceeded to reduce the price-

Mr. Chairman, I am
rising on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. The hon.
member said he is rising on a question of privilege.
Mr. Chairman, my question of privilege is that the minister said I was a member of the government in 19511952. I was not a member of any government in 1951-52.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if
I said that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was a member of the government of that time, of course I overstated the fact.
You misstated the fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member accepted outwardly the role of being a member of the government somewhat later, not thereby evidently increasing his influence. Having regard to the extent to which he seemed to have influenced the strategy of the government in those times I think I am not unfair to the hon. member in ascribing to him a great deal of the responsibility for the blunders and the unjust impositions of that former government even before he accepted a portfolio in the government.
I pointed to the fact that he is spokesman for a party whose government at that time had raised the tax on cigarettes to 25.1 cents per pack and it was the Conservative opposition that demanded that the tax be reduced. Similarly the following year in 1952, and again in 1953, it was the Conservative party, in opposition in those days, which forms the government today that was responsible for keeping up year in and year out the demand that the unfair impositions that the Liberal government was imposing upon the tobacco industry should be eased.
Now you are putting them on again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have indicated why in this present situation with the need for finding further revenues to combat the dangers of inflation, to reduce the deficit and to enable the government to go forward with this recovery program that is gaining momentum day by day and bringing more impetus to the Canadian economy as it proceeds, it is necessary that we recommend to the committee certain increases in taxes now.
No one has pleaded in this chamber the cause of the tobacco grower more effectively, more eloquently or more earnestly than the hon. member for Norfolk. He has been ably supported, as I can testify from my discussions with them, by the hon. members

who represent that cluster of ridings in western Ontario in which tobacco is grown on a substantial scale, including the hon. member for Elgin, the hon. member for Oxford and other hon. members whose voices have been heard and listened to on this subject.
The question has been raised as to whether this very modest increase in the tax on cigarettes and the modest increase in the tax on cigars may have the effect of hurting the interests of the tobacco growers. I do not believe that these very slight increases will have any such effect. We are not in the situation we were in a few years ago.
I have pointed to what happened in the smuggling of United States cigarettes into Canada in the days when the Liberal party was boosting the tax on cigarettes to all-time record heights, and the smuggling went on. If we look at the figures of consumption with respect to cigarettes and have regard to the fact that we have not applied the increase in taxes on tobacco in all forms, I believe hon. members may be re-assured in this regard.
We were careful to confine the increases to tobacco in two forms, cigars and cigarettes. As to cigarettes, may I remind hon. members of the fact that a very heavy increase both in absolute consumption and per capita consumption in cigarettes has occurred in these recent years.
In 1952 when the former government was keeping the tax on cigarettes at a substantially higher figure than it will be under this present budget there were consumed in Canada 18 billion cigarettes, to give the committee round figures. It is estimated that in 1958 the consumption of cigarettes in Canada had increased in round figures to 33 billion. In those six years there had been an increase of nearly 15 billion in the number of cigarettes consumed in Canada and in terms of percentage an increase of 80 per cent in 1958 over the consumption in 1952. Those are absolute figures.
Some hon. member may say there was an increase in population in that period, and that is true. Therefore I give the committee, Mr. Chairman, the per capita figures of consumption of cigarettes in Canada for the same period. In 1952 the per capita consumption of cigarettes in Canada was 1,258. By 1958 that had increased to 1,925. This represents an increase of 667 cigarettes per capita and a percentage increase of 53 per cent in 1958 over 1952.
In the light of the harsh treatment they received under the Liberal government I can well understand why tobacco growers should be vigilant and concerned about any change in their tax treatment. I believe that it is undeniable, however, in the light of these figures

that no modest increase of one-ninth of a cent per cigarette is going to make any impression on these growing figures. I think, therefore, that the tobacco growers of this country can feel quite reassured that this increase is so slight so as to not pose any threat whatever to their interests.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot let one or two observations and especially those of a personal nature made by the minister pass without comment. I do not take the slightest exception to these exaggerated and complimentary references the minister pays to the role I occupied in this country before I became a member of the government but as everyone knows I had no responsibility for preparing any budget even when I was a member of the government except at the very last when I took the collective responsibility that all ministers do.
But even if I did, I would like to remind the committee that the prime minister of that day did not go around before the election promising that the taxes would be reduced and then within 13 months increase them. That is the difference between the Liberal government and the Tory government. The minister knows perfectly well why the tax and other taxes were increased in 1951 and 1952. He knows perfectly well it was because this country was engaged in a war in the Pacific and in the vast rearmament connected with the North Atlantic treaty and for no other reason, and he knows that just as quickly as possible those imposts were reduced.
It is not for me to say whether or not it was too high in 1951, and whether the government was wise to reduce it in 1952 and again in 1953. I imagine they were, but I am sure that those reductions in 1952 and 1953 gave a good deal more pleasure to the people of my native county of Norfolk and other counties round about than this increase they have had and, I repeat, after they had been told at Brantford by the Prime Minister when he was Prime Minister-and I shall read from this same clipping from the Hamilton Spectator:
The tobacco industry has asked for some action, and we are having the question looked into to ascertain what action should be taken to assist the tobacco growers.
This is what they were promised only a year ago in order to get their votes, and this is what they are getting.

Mr. Chairman, I have had an opportunity for over 26 years to listen to ministers of finance, both provincial and federal, and never in those 26 years did I listen to so much financial eyewash as we have had from the present Minister of Finance
Excise Tax Act
in the past few minutes. It is almost inconceivable that the Minister of Finance would have the temerity and audacity to rise in his place and say what he said a few moments ago. He implied-as a matter of fact I can take no other interpretation from it-that all the great works that the government has in mind with respect to social security are tied to this increase in taxation on tobacco. Well, of course, although in the emotionalism of the Minister of Finance that may have been the point, the fact is we spent this afternoon and part of this evening on the Income Tax Act under which authority has been given for increases in taxation.
Of course, the tobacco tax can have no reference whatsoever to old age pension payments, because that also is very carefully covered in the budget, in the resolution and in the bill which will follow. You know, Mr. Chairman, I will admit I have to admire the suavity and-
Gall.
No, I am a gentleman; I would not say gall.
Probity.

I admire the approach of the Minister of Finance. He is one of the most Machiavellian ministers of finance I have yet heard. He can reduce millions of dollars down to one-ninth of one cent. That is very clever, Mr. Chairman, but it is not honesty.
Withdraw.

One second, now; it is true, but not honest. You know why it is not honest? It is true in the presentation of the increase of taxation on one cigarette but it is not honest because it does not give the real picture as to the taxation. I said I gave all respect to a great Machiavellian Minister of Finance but he has not yet answered and I challenge him to answer why. In about two minutes I am going to go out and give the minister one-ninth of one cent increase in the cost of a cigarette because I am going to have a smoke.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Do you think you have earned it?

The important fact is that prior to the speech of the Minister of Finance, through the Minister of National Revenue, he was receiving 54 cents out of every dollar spent in the retail market on cigarettes. He now says his increase is only one-ninth of one cent on a cigarette, but up until now he has been receiving 54 cents out of every dollar spent on cigarettes by the Canadian public. Not being satisfied with 54 cents out of every dollar, he wants to raise the tax so that he gets 56 cents out of every dollar

Excise Tax Act
spent on cigarettes. He speaks of one-ninth of one cent increase on a cigarette. I think the public should know that he is not satisfied with 54 cents out of every dollar; he wants more than that. Surely, there is a limit to what even a minister of finance should ask for as a return.
The minister does not smoke, but the majority of the people of Canada do. Why does he think he has to hit them harder and harder? I do not know why. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, when I see what is happening to the increased taxes on spirits, and to go back to this I must have your permission to speak on what we have already decided, where the government is going to increase the tax so much, I have a dirty, sneaking hunch that very carefully the Minister of Finance is coming pretty close to public ownership because he has taken about everything there is, anyway. He may as well own it and take it all.
That is your platform, not ours.

I was hoping somebody would say that, because, having regard to the way liquor and cigarettes are taxed, you may as well take it all and receive it all. That is the actual situation now, but you have not the intestinal fortitude to own up to it. You are taxing so much now on certain items that you may as well take it all anyway. I do want to say most sincerely that the attitude of the Minister of Finance in going so far as to increase the tax on cigarettes is not fair. He should deal with the amount his government is receiving. I say most sincerely that the 54 per cent already being collected on the sale of cigarettes should be enough for a private enterprise government to collect. I would ask that consideration be given to letting the average citizen enjoy his smokes and his liquor too, if you wish, without the government collecting any more unless the government has the fortitude to come out and say that they will take over both of them under public ownership.

I should like to ask one question of the minister. On December 20, 1957 the Minister of National Revenue said that he was recommending a change in the regulations governing the exemption from tax of cigarettes on fishing vessels. Up till that time the tax was not imposed if the vessels were out of port for 15 days and he said he was reducing it to 10 days. This was a pretty slender implementation of the very high hopes held out on the east coast by members of the Conservative party in the 1957 election but one has to admit that they did do a little something about it. I wonder whether the

minister can assure us that at least that small concession is not being taken away at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The proposed
change in the act will not affect the regulations.
I appreciate that but I was asking the minister if he could give us the assurance that there was no thought of changing that regulation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I certainly have heard of none and I do not believe there is any thought of making any such change.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a very few words about this matter. As the representative of a constituency which is at the very heart of the flue-cured and cigar tobacco producing area of Quebec, I feel sure that this increase is only temporary and that in the near future, perhaps next year, the minister will reconsider his policy, and cut the excise tax on cigar and cigarette tobaccos.
It is too bad that, under the Liberal administration, the excise tax on cigar and cigarette tobaccos went up by 100 per cent.
I am equally sure that nobody is more anxious than the Minister of Finance to help the tobacco grower. So I would ask him to consider the possibility of raising the tariff on cigar tobaccos imported from the United States or Cuba.
The most unfortunate part of it, under the former administration, was that customs duties on non-manufactured cigar tobacco were considerably lowered. For instance, in 1936, the rate on unstemmed cigar tobacco leaves was 40 cents a pound and on stemmed tobacco 60 cents a pound. On January 1, 1948, the custom duty on unstemmed tobacco went down to 20 cents a pound, and to 30 cents a pound, for stemmed tobacco. On October 17, 1948, duty rates on unstemmed and stemmed tobacco were decreased to 15 cents and 22J cents respectively. On June 30, 1956, the customs duty on unstemmed tobacco and stemmed tobacco went down to 12J and 20 cents a pound respectively.
Mr. Chairman, I may assure you that I have witnessed the effect of those lowered customs duty rates. Cigar tobacco producers in the province of Quebec came to Ottawa on various occasions and made representations to the government of the day, asking that the customs duties be raised. But they were always turned down.

Mr. Chairman, I am asking the Minister of Finance to study the possibility of raising customs duties in respect of tobacco imported from the United States and Cuba.
I know that the excise tax increase on tobacco is only a temporary one. The present government incurred a slight deficit due to the poor administration which preceded it, but I am satisfied that the budgetary position, and the balance of the budget will be restored under the present administration, because we have at the head of the finance department a most able and efficient man.
Before concluding my brief remarks, Mr. Chairman, I again ask the Minister of Finance to consider whether it would be possible to increase customs duties on imported tobacco and within the near future, to abolish excise duties on cigars while lowering the excise tax on cigarettes.

Mr. Chairman, I listened very closely and with much interest to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). I noted that the hon. member supported the opposition, in the sense that he was so opposed to the increased excise tax on cigarettes that he had the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) practically promise that the increase was only temporary, which means that it would be removed next year, if we are to believe the hon. member for J oliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.
Like members of the present government, when the hon. member is in a tight spot, he talks about the misdeeds of the previous government. On the other hand, when he wishes to speak well of his own party, he readily reverts to the times of Sir John A. Macdonald. However, few Conservative members from the province of Quebec will boast of their traditional ties with the administration of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm complained of the fact that, under the Liberal administration, some associations asked for a cut in customs duties on cigar tobacco-
They asked that the duty be raised.

Those associations are said to have asked that the customs duties be raised.
Now, I understand this government has been in power for twenty months. It went through two elections with considerable success. Then, how is it the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, with his influence, has not been able to convince the present government to raise the customs duties? People come here in this house and
Excise Tax Act
complain, discuss taxation, and quote figures applying to the past five, six and even ten years. They talk about the past, but not about the present-
They should be talking about the future.

Why does not the government act as if it were alive at this moment and as if it were really running the country, not only in relation to the past, but in relation to the present? When will it finally quit accusing every one except itself? And when will it stop boasting?
The hon. Minister of Finance asked us a moment ago to support this motion, stating that it will only involve a minor increase. The hon. member for Joliette-l'Assomption-Montcalm said there was only a "small deficit". Would you call $617,000,000 a small deficit? As the member who spoke before me has indicated, it is really a 56 per cent tax on the price of cigarettes.
Furthermore, in replying to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill), the hon. Minister of Finance completely evaded the issue. He simply said that the Conservative government had made many promises, and that not only had such promises not been kept but that the government had actually taken opposite steps. We have heard the Minister of Finance say that taxes were raised in 1952, and again in 1953 and 1954. He quoted percentage ratios, etc., and gave that as an answer to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In short, I am convinced he spoke for about 15 minutes without replying to the objections and criticisms raised by the hon. member. Every time this government is in trouble, the minister avoids replying to questions. He speaks for three hours, and quotes masses of figures so that no one will be able to make heads or tails out of it. The fact remains that he has raised the tax after promising to reduce it.
Is it not a fact that this famous customs duty is still the same, and that there has been no increase, despite anything the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm may say? What is their purpose in accusing the former administration of doing worse, or just as bad, when they had promised to do better? They have been in power twenty months; so they have had time to correct any past mistakes.
This tax increase is the responsibility of the Conservative government. I therefore ask the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm to swallow his pill, and if because there is no increase in the customs duty on tobacco, and his constituents have to suffer

Excise Tax Act
hardship through the fault of his government, let him take the responsibility.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I am considerably surprised that the Minister of Finance would propose this change in the law. I realize that he needs the revenue very much but I thought, in view of what he had said in previous years and what his colleagues had said, he was thoroughly conversant with the law of diminishing returns. I thought he would benefit from the experience of his predecessors who found that sometimes when taxes are increased this results in a lower yield to the government than would have been returned had the taxes remained at a lower level.
It was with considerable surprise, therefore, that we listened to the minister tell us in his budget speech that he was going to repeat something that in earlier years he told us was a mistake and which again tonight he told us was a mistake. This is something about which he spoke very strongly and very vigorously in earlier days and which he characterized as another error and more fumbling on the part of the then administration. Still he walks right into the same trap. We are additionally surprised because of the sentiments expressed by members of the government during the election campaign. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has mentioned some of the things that were said in the tobacco growing district. I have another quotation here which I should like to put on the record. This is from the Globe and Mail and the dateline is Brantford, February 17, 1958. It reads as follows:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker last night dropped a clear hint that the taxes on cigarettes, cigars and tobacco soon may be cut.
He told an audience of 1,400 that no industry in Canada suffers a greater degree of taxation than the tobacco industry-
To the Brantford audience, living on the northern fringe of Ontario's tobacco belt-where production has jumped from 63,000 acres in 1943 to 120,000 in 1956-the Prime Minister's hint appeared an effective vote catcher.
The Minister of Finance has told us tonight that the hon. member for Norfolk has made representations on behalf of the tobacco growing industry, and that they had listened to him. Obviously he did not speak loudly enough or clearly enough to get through to the Minister of Finance. It is, therefore, necessary for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and myself, because we are also natives of Norfolk county, to come to his assistance. I should like to move:
That paragraph 1 be striken out of the resolution and that the following paragraphs be renumbered accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Obviously, such an
amendment is out of order; it is a straight negative.

I should like to say a word on the point raised by the Minister of Finance. The minister says this amendment is a straight negative. The minister knows, of course, quite well that this is a resolution to amend the Excise Tax Act and all these seven paragraphs compose the one resolution. He knows quite well that the effect of striking out one paragraph is not to negative the resolution but is merely to reduce the amount of the total change in the tax, the amount of increase in the tax. I think even the minister will admit that one of the rights of parliament that is perhaps more sacred than any other is the right to vote taxes or to vote against taxes. The suggestion that it is incompetent to any member to vote that a part of the tax be reduced is surely too preposterous for the Chair to entertain. This would be the effect of the amendment. We are not asking the committee to strike out the whole thing; we are asking them to strike out one paragraph to reduce the amount of the increase. I submit, sir, that the amendment is in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we have been taking up each of these resolutions paragraph by paragraph. What is before the committee now is paragraph 1 of the resolution respecting the Excise Tax Act. What is introduced now by the hon. member for Trinity is an amendment to strike out paragraph 1 which is now under discussion, and to renumber the balance of the paragraphs. With respect to the matter now before the committee, which is the paragraph, obviously the amendment is straight negative and therefore out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Trinity is that paragraph 1 be striken out of the resolution and the following paragraphs be renumbered accordingly. After consulting Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 221, citation 265, I find it reads:
No member other than a minister of the crown may introduce a bill for the reduction of duties. The government must take full responsibility for the taxation levied to provide the revenue. But the house enjoys complete freedom to make every representation possible to the government with regard to the manner in which the ministers discharge this responsibility. This duty the members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the administration.
If the purpose of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Trinity is that taxes may be reduced, then in my opinion the amendment is in order. If the purpose is that the tax may be removed altogether by removing paragraph 1, then the amendment is not in order.
If I may say a word on the point of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Trinity should explain more clearly the purpose of his amendment.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, this
amendment does not remove or eliminate the tax on cigarettes. All it does is to reduce the proposed increase in taxes contained in this resolution, and as such it is merely part of the proposed total increase in taxation presented to the committee by the minister. Consequently it is in effect a reduction in taxation and therefore clearly falls within the last part of the citation from Beauchesne, and is in my opinion in order.

May I refer you, Mr. Chairman, to paragraph 202, page 170, subsection (15):
(15) An amendment approving part of a motion and disapproving the remainder is out of order.
I would submit that in this particular case to agree to this motion would be to split the motion and thus be in breach of this particular clause.

On that point, may I say that this amendment does not say anything about the other paragraphs, whether they are approved or disapproved. The resolution before the committee is a single resolution. The word "resolved" appears only once. The hon. member for Trinity has moved that the first paragraph, which is a part and only a part of the total increase in taxes proposed, should be stricken out. He is not moving that the rest of the taxes be stricken out. It therefore seems to me that it is in strict conformity with the citation that Your Honour read:
This duty the members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the administration.
The administration has proposed to increase the excise tax in a number of ways. We are suggesting that in one of these ways the increase should not take place and therefore the total should be reduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is an extremely ingenious argument that has just been addressed to you, Mr. Chairman. You invited the hon. member for Trinity to explain the purpose of his amendment. He says that he wishes to eliminate the proposed tax increase in paragraph 1. He does not deal with his attitude toward the remaining paragraphs in the resolution. Then along comes the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and says, "Oh, this is just one resolution. We are just dealing with one change in one aspect of the resolution". But,
Excise Tax Act
Mr. Chairman, this is intended to evade the point of your question. Unless the purpose of the amendment is to adopt the balance of the resolution, there is no escape from the point I have addressed to you, namely that this is in effect a negative because we are dealing only with the first paragraph thus far. That is what was called.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If this can be done on the first paragraph, then when we come to paragraph 2 the hon. gentlemen could move to strike out paragraph No. 2 and rearrange the numbering. Then when we come to paragraph 3, they could move to strike it out and renumber the other paragraphs. Then when we come to paragraph No. 4, they could move to strike it out and renumber the balance. Then when we come to paragraph 5, they could move to strike it out and renumber the remaining ones. They could do the same with regard to paragraph 6 and paragraph 7. In that way they would have established seven different negatives. Obviously that procedure defies reason. It defies the rules of the house.
The plainest rule of the house is that no amendment can be introduced which is in effect a negative to a motion. It is a most ingenious argument to say, "We are dealing only with one part of this resolution and the rest of it stands". But, Mr. Chairman, the rest of it does not stand. They are reserving the right to come along and do the same thing with regard to every other paragraph. Surely that is the answer to what they are saying.
I give you the citation in Beauchesne's fourth edition at page 222. It is citation 266 subparagraph (4) which reads as follows:
(4) It is not in order to move the deletion of a particular clause in an excise tax resolution because it alters the balance of ways and means. Chairman's decision confirmed by the house on a division-
That was in 1951. I well remember the case because the situation there was that an opposition member moved to strike out a certain proposed tax and the motion was ruled out of order. Then an attempt was made by an ingenious member to overcome that difficulty by saying, "Oh, we will take this tax off and we will put on another in its place so that the balance of ways and means shall not be disturbed." That procedure was ruled not to save the situation. It was ruled out of order. I suggest that this amendment, a much clearer case than that in 1951, is out of order because it is clearly a negative.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If I may be allowed to reply to what my hon. friend has said, Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring to your attention

Excise Tax Act
the fact that if the minister's argument were to be accepted, we on this side of the house could at no time move to reduce a tax as has been done by the hon. member for Trinity. After all, surely there are still some rights left on this side of the house. What we are doing in effect is making a motion to leave the tax exactly where it was before this resolution was introduced and to leave the remaining paragraphs of that resolution exactly as they are, renumbering them as the amendment states. I think the situation is covered clearly, not only by citation 265, the latter part of which you have brought to the attention of the committee, but also by citation 244, subsection (2), where motions and amendments of this nature have been held to be in order. If the argument of the minister were to be accepted, we on this side of the house could never make a motion to reduce a tax; and I am sure that is not the intention of those who made the rules of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend wishes to establish the fact that he is against the proposed increase, then under the rules of the house he divides the house on this motion. There is no excuse whatever for introducing an amendment that is in effect a straight negative.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not like the division. That is the trouble.

With respect, Mr. Chairman, may I point out to hon. members opposite that we are here dealing with a ways and means resolution. They have been quoting from Beauchesne on matters dealing with other types of motions. I would respectfully submit that citation 266 is the only one that is germane. We are dealing with a ways and means resolution. Therefore citation 266 (4) as cited by the minister is completely applicable and that should be the ruling.

On the point made by
the hon. member for Edmonton West, may I say this. The only way in which a tax change can be made is by a ways and means resolution. What the hon. member is saying is that the citation which Your Honour read as the most relevant one does not mean anything at all. It is impossible that Your Honour could have been so mistaken.

Order. This point of procedure has somewhat complicated my existence tonight. Many points of view on this matter have been expressed. It is my opinion that, in accordance with paragraph 265 (1), this duty members may perform by moving amendments to reduce the taxes proposed by the administration. Actually, it is my personal opinion that the amendment moved by

the hon. member for Trinity has been badly framed and is not explicit enough. For instance, it is quite obvious that if paragraph 1 were eliminated by the committee, the succeeding paragraphs would move up one, that paragraph 2 would become paragraph 1 and so on. If actually the desire of the hon. member for Trinity and his colleagues in the opposition is that the taxes be reduced to their former level, their amendment should have been written in such a way as to imply as much.
As I understand it at present, there have been many decisions on this matter of an amendment in the past which are similar to this one. I have in front of me a ruling which was made in the House of Commons in Westminster, and there are other rulings available which may be somewhat contradictory. Therefore, if it is agreeable to the house I would like to consult over this matter and render a decision tomorrow based on the various facts and authorities which will be collected. Shall we then proceed with paragraph 2 and revert to paragraph 1 tomorrow when such decision will have been reached?

That suggestion will be agreeable to us, Mr. Chairman.
Paragraph stands.
Paragraphs 2 and 3 agreed.
On paragraph 4.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there any discussion on paragraph 4?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to reiterate what I said in the budget speech about the changing of the tax level from the manufacturer to the packager, and about the discrimination between certain types of retail outlets. With this in view anything I may say refers to the cosmetic field, the same as it does to the pharmaceutical field. A level of the tax where you put the packager into the manufacturers' level is creating discrimination between retail outlets. Should a retailer be able to buy in sufficient quantities from the manufacturer and pay the sales tax at his level, he would naturally be paying 11 per cent tax. But when the packager who is now classified as a manufacturer buys the same product from the manufacturer and turns it out to his retail outlet plus his own costs, he would have to include it in his costs and turn it over to a retail outlet not within his own company. I am speaking of a wholesaler when I say this. He must take into account in his packaging the cost of his bottle, his label, his labour and his control. I am advised by one of the largest retailing and wholesale outfits in Canada, certainly

one of the largest under the same roof in the North American continent, that the cost to his retail outlet will be exactly doubled. For argument's sake, if the cost of tablets, say, at the manufacturing level, was $1, by the time he would receive and package them the cost would increase to $2. Therefore the pass-on would be 22 cents as against 11 cents in the case of $1.
I am reiterating what I said, Mr. Chairman, in the budget debate, that this tax is discriminatory as between certain types of outlets. I am now speaking about where there is no wholesaler in between a manufacturer and his retail outlet. In other words, certain large organizations would buy in the necessary quantities required from the manufacturer. They could do their packaging in their own warehouse or in their retail store, it would make no difference. It would still be under the same organization, and they in turn could sell to the consumer at manufacturer's cost or his 11 per cent mark-up. He would have an advantage over the packager, whom I will call the wholesaler, who would have to add the extra tax to his cost of doing business before it is passed on to his retail outlet over which he has no control.
I claim that this is discrimination and is to the advantage of the larger organizations, and certainly to the disadvantage of the smaller retailer. Any way you look at it, Mr. Chairman, the cost of this merchandise to the eventual consumer is increased. If it goes through a wholesaler who is now classified as a packager and in the same category as a manufacturer, the tax is collected at a higher level. Therefore the tax being passed on naturally has to be at a higher level to the person who is retailing it to his customer.
I do not think the minister feels this is the proper approach to this, because it is favouring some sides of the retail outlet and is discriminating against others who have not
Business of the House
the in-between facilities, shall I say, that the larger retailer would have. There is many an outlet from coast to coast, Mr. Chairman, which has one purchasing unit and does not need to pass on the tax through a wholesaler but instead passes it on through its own organization, whether they package it in their own warehouse or in their own retail outlet, be it at Vancouver or Halifax. They are not in the same category as the so-called packager who is being classified as a manufacturer, but the tax is assessed at the manufacturers' or packagers' cost rather than at the retailers' cost, which seems to me is an increase in tax of over 100 per cent.
